games.title: Real wealth?
items: The people of a country are called its real wealth.
They use resources and make policies.
Population is evenly spread over the earth's surface.
Population growth was always fast throughout history.
It was slow for a long time and fast only recently.
Composition is one of the aspects in which population is studied.

quiz.q: Why are the people of a country called its real wealth?
options: They own all the minerals personally
They use its resources and make its policies
quiz.explain: People turn resources into wealth and shape decisions, so they are the real wealth.
steps: Asked: why people are a country's real wealth.
Lesson: people use the country's resources and decide its policies.
So the answer is that they use its resources and make its policies.
Answer: They use its resources and make its policies
quiz.mistake: Thinks wealth means only money or minerals

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four aspects in which population is usually studied?
quiz.explain: Population is studied by distribution, density, growth and composition. Altitude is a physical feature.
steps: The four aspects: distribution, density, growth and composition.
Altitude is not in the list — it is a physical feature of land.
So altitude is the answer.
Answer: Altitude
quiz.mistake: Adds a physical feature to the list

quiz.q: 'The way people are spaced over the earth's surface' defines:
quiz.explain: Distribution is about pattern of spacing; density is a ratio of people to area.
steps: Asked: the term for how people are spaced over the earth's surface.
Lesson: that is distribution.
Density is a ratio (people per sq km), so it does not fit the definition.
Answer: Distribution of population

quiz.q: World population crossed which mark in November 2022, according to the UN?
quiz.explain: The UN announced the world reached 8 billion on 15 November 2022.
steps: Asked: the mark crossed in November 2022.
Lesson: the UN marked world population crossing 8 billion then.
So the answer is 8 billion.
Answer: 8 billion

quiz.q: Which statement about historical world population growth is correct?
options: It has been rapid at a constant rate since prehistoric times
It was slow for a long time and became very rapid in recent centuries
It has fallen continuously since the 1800s
quiz.explain: Growth was slow in early periods and speeded up after the Industrial Revolution.
steps: Asked: the correct trend of growth over history.
Lesson: growth was slow for most of history and very fast in recent centuries.
So 'slow for a long time, then very rapid' is correct.
Answer: It was slow for a long time and became very rapid in recent centuries

quiz.q: Assertion (A): A country is ultimately known by its people. Reason (R): People use the country's resources and decide its policies.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; because people are the users of resources and makers of policy, a country is identified by them.
steps: Check A: a country is known by its people — true.
Check R: people use resources and decide policies — true.
Because people run the country, it is identified by them, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks R is unrelated to A

quiz.q: Which pair is correct for the study of population?
options: Distribution — people per unit area; Density — spacing of people
Distribution — spacing of people; Density — people per unit area
Growth — sex ratio; Composition — birth rate
quiz.explain: Distribution = pattern of spacing; density = ratio of people to land area.
steps: Distribution = spacing of people over the earth's surface.
Density = people per unit area.
Only the option 'Distribution — spacing; Density — people per unit area' matches.
Answer: Distribution — spacing of people; Density — people per unit area

quiz.q: A map shows dots crowded along the Ganga valley and few dots in the Thar desert. This map mainly shows population:
quiz.explain: A dot map showing where people live shows distribution.
steps: The map shows where people are crowded (Ganga valley) and where few live (Thar).
Showing where people live is population distribution.
It shows no change over time, so it is not growth.
Answer: Distribution
quiz.mistake: Thinks any population map shows growth

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What does population distribution mean, and in what other ways do geographers study population?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Distribution, density, growth and composition — four lenses to look at people!
teach.nudge: Good! What are the other aspects besides distribution?

revise.summary: A country's people are its real wealth because they use its resources and make its policies. World population crossed 8 billion in November 2022, and geographers study it by distribution, density, growth and composition.
focus: The four aspects: distribution, density, growth and composition
Telling distribution (spacing of people) from density (people per unit area)
Why people are called the real wealth of a country
remember: Population is studied by distribution, density, growth and composition
Distribution = the way people are spaced over the earth's surface
World population crossed 8 billion in November 2022 (UN)
traps: Don't swap distribution and density — density is a ratio of people to area
Don't think world population always grew fast — it was slow for most of history

learn.hook: Nine out of ten people on Earth squeeze into just one-tenth of its land. Where are they all?
points: About 90 per cent of the world's population lives in about 10 per cent of its land area.
The 10 most populous countries contribute about 60 per cent of world population; 6 of these 10 are in Asia.
India and China together hold over a third of humanity; India became the most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate).
On a world map, densely populated belts lie in East, South and South-east Asia, north-western Europe and north-eastern USA; sparse areas lie near the poles, in deserts and in equatorial rainforests.

example.q: If world population is 8 billion, about how many people live on 10 per cent of the land?
steps: About 90% of people live on 10% of land.
90% of 8 billion = 0.9 × 8 = 7.2 billion.
example.answer: About 7.2 billion

learn.reallife: India's population is about 18 per cent of the world but on only about 2.4 per cent of world land — a classic example of uneven distribution.

games.title: Distribution facts
items: About 90% of the world's population lives in about 10% of its land area.
Of the 10 most populous countries, 6 are in Asia.
The 10 most populous countries hold about 25% of world population.
Antarctica is one of the densely populated regions.

quiz.q: About what share of the world's population lives in about 10 per cent of its land area?
quiz.explain: Population is very unevenly spread: about 90% live on about 10% of land.
steps: Asked: share of people living on about 10% of land.
Lesson: about 90% of the world's population lives on about 10% of its land.
So the answer is 90%; 60% is the top-10 countries' share.
Answer: 90%
quiz.mistake: Confuses this with the 60% share of the top 10 countries

quiz.q: The 10 most populous countries together contribute about what share of world population?
quiz.explain: NCERT notes the top 10 countries contribute about 60%.
steps: Asked: share of world population in the 10 most populous countries.
Lesson: about 60%.
90% is the land-concentration figure, so it is wrong here.
Answer: 60%
quiz.mistake: Picks the 90% figure meant for land concentration

quiz.q: How many of the 10 most populous countries are located in Asia?
quiz.explain: Six of the ten most populous countries are in Asia.
steps: Asked: how many of the top 10 countries are in Asia.
Lesson: 6 of the 10 most populous countries are in Asia.
So the answer is 6.
Answer: 6

quiz.q: If the world has 8 billion people, roughly how many billion people live in the 10 most populous countries (about 60%)?
quiz.explain: 60% of 8 billion = 0.6 × 8 = 4.8 billion.
steps: 0.6 × 8 = 4.8 billion
Answer: 4.8

quiz.q: On a world population map, which area would appear sparsely populated?
quiz.explain: Hot deserts like the Sahara have very few people.
steps: Sparse areas: near the poles, hot and cold deserts, equatorial rainforests.
The interior of the Sahara is a hot desert.
Ganga plains, north-eastern USA and eastern China are dense belts.
Answer: Interior of the Sahara

quiz.q: Which continent has the largest number of the world's most populous countries?
quiz.explain: Asia has 6 of the top 10.
steps: Lesson: 6 of the 10 most populous countries are in Asia.
No other continent has as many.
So the answer is Asia.
Answer: Asia
quiz.mistake: Thinks Africa leads because of high growth rates

quiz.q: Assertion (A): World population distribution is highly uneven. Reason (R): About 90 per cent of people live in about 10 per cent of the land area.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true, and R is the data that shows A.
steps: Check A: distribution is highly uneven — true.
Check R: about 90% live on about 10% of land — true.
That statistic is the evidence of unevenness, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the statistic and the unevenness are unrelated

quiz.q: Which country became the world's most populous in 2023, according to UN estimates?
quiz.explain: UN estimates showed India overtaking China in 2023.
steps: Asked: country that became most populous in 2023.
Lesson: UN estimates show India overtook China in 2023.
So the answer is India.
Answer: India

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Is the world's population spread evenly? Give me some numbers.'
teach.praise: Chirp! 90% of people on 10% of land — that's really crowded!
teach.nudge: Good! Can you give the 90% / 10% fact, and say where most people live?

revise.summary: World population is very unevenly spread: about 90% of people live on about 10% of the land. The 10 most populous countries hold about 60% of people, 6 of them in Asia, and India became the most populous country in 2023.
focus: The 90% on 10% of land figure and the 60% top-10 figure
Dense belts vs sparse areas on a world map
Asia's share of the most populous countries
remember: About 90% of people live on about 10% of the land
10 most populous countries ≈ 60% of world population; 6 of the 10 are in Asia
India became the most populous country in 2023 (UN estimate)
traps: Don't mix the 90% (land concentration) with the 60% (top 10 countries)
Sparse areas are near the poles, in deserts and in equatorial rainforests — not north-eastern USA

learn.hook: Bihar packs over 1,100 people into each square kilometre; Arunachal Pradesh, about 17. Same country, very different crowding!
points: Density of population = number of people ÷ area of land; expressed as persons per sq km.
Example: a region of 100 sq km with 1,50,000 people has density 1,50,000 ÷ 100 = 1,500 persons per sq km.
Densely populated regions: north-eastern USA, north-western Europe, and South, South-east and East Asia.
Sparsely populated regions: areas near the North and South Poles, hot and cold deserts, and high rainfall zones near the equator.
Medium density regions: western China, southern India, Norway and Sweden.

example.q: District A has 24,00,000 people on 1,200 sq km. District B has 9,00,000 people on 300 sq km. Which is denser?
steps: Density B = 9,00,000 ÷ 300 = 3,000 per sq km.
B is denser even though it has fewer people.
example.answer: District B (3,000 per sq km)

learn.reallife: Census 2011 recorded India's density as 382 persons per sq km — Delhi topped among states/UTs, while Arunachal Pradesh was the lowest.

items.q: A density of 500 on 20 sq km means how many people?

quiz.q: Density of population is expressed as:
quiz.explain: Density is a ratio of people to land area, so the unit is persons per sq km.
steps: Asked: the unit of density.
Density = people ÷ land area.
So it is expressed as persons per sq km, not per year.
Answer: Persons per sq km
quiz.mistake: Confuses density with growth rate or birth rate

quiz.q: A region has an area of 100 sq km and a population of 1,50,000. What is its density (persons per sq km)?
quiz.explain: Density = 1,50,000 ÷ 100 = 1,500 persons per sq km.
steps: Density = population ÷ area
1,50,000 ÷ 100 = 1,500 persons per sq km
Answer: 1,500
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of dividing, or misplaces zeros

quiz.q: A taluka of 250 sq km has a density of 600 persons per sq km. What is its population?
quiz.explain: Population = density × area = 600 × 250 = 1,50,000.
steps: Population = density × area
Answer: 1,50,000
quiz.mistake: Divides or adds instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Which of these is a medium density region of the world?
quiz.explain: NCERT lists western China, southern India, Norway and Sweden as medium density.
steps: Lesson: medium density regions are western China, southern India, Norway and Sweden.
North-eastern USA and Bangladesh are dense; polar regions are sparse.
So the answer is Norway and Sweden.
Answer: Norway and Sweden

quiz.q: Which is NOT a sparsely populated region?
options: High rainfall zones near the equator
quiz.explain: North-western Europe is densely populated; the others are sparse.
steps: Sparse: near the poles, cold and hot deserts, equatorial high rainfall zones.
North-western Europe is listed as densely populated.
So north-western Europe is NOT sparse.
Answer: North-western Europe
quiz.mistake: Thinks all cold places are sparse, including Europe

quiz.q: Town P: 6,00,000 people on 200 sq km. Town Q: 8,00,000 people on 400 sq km. By how many persons per sq km is P's density greater than Q's?
quiz.explain: P = 3,000 and Q = 2,000 persons per sq km, so P is denser by 1,000.
steps: Answer: 1,000
quiz.mistake: Compares total populations instead of densities

quiz.q: Assertion (A): High rainfall zones near the equator are sparsely populated. Reason (R): Dense forests, heat and humidity make settlement and farming difficult there.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the harsh conditions of equatorial rainforests explain the sparse population.
steps: Check A: equatorial high rainfall zones are sparse — true.
Check R: dense forest, heat and humidity make settling and farming hard — true.
Those harsh conditions cause the low population, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks heavy rain always means dense farming population

quiz.q: Which region is among the most densely populated in the world?
quiz.explain: South, South-east and East Asia are among the most densely populated regions.
steps: Dense regions: north-eastern USA, north-western Europe, South, South-east and East Asia.
Central Australia, Siberia and Greenland are large but nearly empty.
So South Asia is the answer.
Answer: South Asia
quiz.mistake: Picks a large but empty region

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How do you calculate population density, and where in the world is it high or low?'
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! People divided by area — and Asia is packed while the poles are empty!
teach.nudge: Nice! Give the formula for density and name one dense and one sparse region.

revise.summary: Density of population = number of people ÷ area, in persons per sq km. Dense regions include north-eastern USA, north-western Europe and South, South-east and East Asia; sparse regions are polar areas, deserts and equatorial rainforests.
focus: Calculating density, and population from density × area
Classifying regions as dense, medium or sparse
Comparing densities rather than total populations
remember: Density = population ÷ area (persons per sq km)
Dense: north-eastern USA, north-western Europe, South, South-east and East Asia
Medium: western China, southern India, Norway, Sweden
Sparse: near the poles, hot and cold deserts, high rainfall zones near the equator
traps: Don't multiply population by area to get density — divide
A place with more people is not always denser; compare people per sq km

learn.hook: Why did the great civilisations grow along the Nile, the Indus and the Hwang He? Follow the water.
points: Availability of water: people prefer areas where fresh water is easily available; river valleys are among the most densely populated areas.
Landforms: people prefer flat plains and gentle slopes, which suit farming, roads and industry. Ganga plains are densely populated; mountains like the Andes, Alps and Himalayas are sparse.
Climate: extreme climates such as very hot or cold deserts are uncomfortable; areas with a comfortable climate with little seasonal variation, like Mediterranean regions, attract people.
Soils: fertile loamy soils support intensive agriculture, so plains of the Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He and Chang Jiang (in China) are densely populated.

example.q: Explain why the Ganga plains are far more crowded than Ladakh.
steps: Water: perennial Ganga and tributaries vs scarce water in Ladakh.
Landform: flat plain vs high mountains.
Climate and soil: moderate climate and fertile alluvium vs cold desert and thin soils.
example.answer: Water, flat land, fertile soil and moderate climate make the Ganga plains densely populated

learn.reallife: The Indo-Gangetic plain supports some of the world's highest rural densities thanks to rivers, alluvial soil and canal irrigation.

games.title: Factor and example
pairs: Fertile loamy plains of the Nile and Chang Jiang

games.title: Geography decides
items: Mountains like the Alps and Andes are densely populated.
Fertile loamy soils support intensive agriculture.
That is why alluvial river plains are crowded.
Hot and cold deserts have extreme climates that discourage settlement.
Discomfort and difficulty of farming keep numbers low.
River valleys are among the least populated parts of the world.
They are among the most densely populated.

quiz.q: Which geographical factor explains why river valleys are among the most densely populated areas?
quiz.explain: Fresh water for drinking, farming and transport draws people to river valleys.
steps: Asked: why river valleys are densely populated.
Lesson: people prefer areas where fresh water is easily available.
So the factor is availability of water.
Answer: Availability of water
quiz.mistake: Picks an economic or social factor

quiz.q: Why are the Himalayas, Andes and Alps sparsely populated?
options: Rugged landforms make farming, transport and settlement difficult
quiz.explain: Steep slopes and harsh terrain discourage settlement.
steps: Asked: why the Himalayas, Andes and Alps are sparse.
Lesson: people prefer flat land; rugged mountains make farming, transport and settlement hard.
So the answer is rugged landforms.
Answer: Rugged landforms make farming, transport and settlement difficult

quiz.q: Which plains are cited for fertile loamy soils and dense population?
options: Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He and Chang Jiang
quiz.explain: These alluvial river plains support intensive farming.
steps: Asked: plains with fertile loamy soils and dense population.
Lesson: Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He and Chang Jiang plains.
Sahara, Thar and tundra are sparse, so they are wrong.
Answer: Nile, Ganga, Hwang-He and Chang Jiang

quiz.q: Which climate type has historically attracted people due to its pleasantness?
quiz.explain: The comfortable Mediterranean climate attracted people from early times.
steps: Asked: climate that attracted people for its pleasantness.
Lesson: comfortable climates with little seasonal change, like the Mediterranean, attract people.
So the answer is Mediterranean.
Answer: Mediterranean
quiz.mistake: Thinks hot deserts are attractive due to sunshine

quiz.q: A region is flat, has fertile alluvium and a perennial river, but is in a cold desert. Which factor would most limit its population?
quiz.explain: All other factors are favourable; the extreme cold climate is the limiting factor.
steps: Check each factor: flat land ✓, fertile alluvium ✓, perennial river ✓.
Only the climate (cold desert) is unfavourable.
So climate is the limiting factor.
Answer: Climate

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Plains are preferred for human settlement. Reason (R): They are suitable for agriculture, construction of roads and industries.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the ease of farming and building on flat land explains the preference.
steps: Check A: plains are preferred for settlement — true.
Check R: they suit agriculture, roads and industries — true.
That ease of use is why people prefer plains, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect ease of use to settlement

quiz.q: Which of these is a geographical (not economic or social) factor of population distribution?
quiz.explain: Water, landforms, climate and soils are geographical factors.
steps: Geographical factors: water, landforms, climate, soils.
Urbanisation and industrialisation are economic; religious importance is cultural.
So the answer is soils.
Answer: Soils
quiz.mistake: Treats urbanisation as a geographical factor

quiz.q: Which pairing correctly explains low population in the Thar desert?
quiz.explain: The Thar has a hot, dry climate and scarce water.
steps: The Thar is a hot desert.
Its limits are an extreme climate and scarce water.
Rugged mountains and dense forests describe other regions, not the Thar.
Answer: Extreme climate and scarce water
quiz.mistake: Applies mountain or rainforest reasons to a desert

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What natural factors decide where people live?' Name and explain at least three.
teach.praise: Chirp! Water, land, climate and soil — nature's four magnets!
teach.nudge: Good! You missed one — think about water, landforms, climate and soils.

revise.summary: Geographical factors shape where people live: fresh water, flat plains, a comfortable climate and fertile soils attract people, so river valleys and plains like the Ganga are crowded, while mountains, deserts and polar areas are sparse.
focus: The four geographical factors: water, landforms, climate, soils
Using factors to explain dense vs sparse areas
Finding the limiting factor in a case
remember: River valleys are among the most densely populated areas because of fresh water
Plains and gentle slopes suit farming, roads and industry; mountains (Andes, Alps, Himalayas) are sparse

learn.hook: Jamshedpur grew from a forest village to a steel city in a few decades. What pulled people there?
points: Minerals: areas with mineral deposits attract industries, and mining and industrial activity create jobs; e.g. the Katanga-Zambia copper belt in Africa.
Urbanisation: cities offer better civic amenities, employment, education, medical facilities and transport, so they attract rural-urban migrants and grow large.
Industrialisation: industrial belts provide jobs for factory workers and also transport operators, shopkeepers, bank staff, doctors and teachers; e.g. Kobe-Osaka region of Japan.

Social and cultural factors: places of religious or cultural significance attract people (Varanasi, Jerusalem, Vatican City); social and political unrest pushes people out; governments sometimes offer incentives to settle sparse areas.

example.q: Classify: (i) Jharia coalfield town grows; (ii) pilgrims settle in Varanasi; (iii) people leave a conflict-hit region; (iv) Gurugram's offices draw graduates.
steps: (i) Minerals → economic.
(ii) Religious significance → social/cultural.
(iii) Unrest → social/political push.
(iv) Urban jobs and amenities → economic (urbanisation).
example.answer: (i) economic, (ii) cultural, (iii) social-political, (iv) economic (urbanisation)

learn.reallife: Migrants from Bihar and UP to Mumbai, Surat and Delhi follow jobs created by industrialisation and urbanisation.

quiz.q: The Kobe-Osaka region of Japan is densely populated mainly due to:
quiz.explain: NCERT cites Kobe-Osaka as an industrial belt that attracts large numbers of people.
steps: Asked: why the Kobe-Osaka region is dense.
Lesson: it is cited as an industrial belt that attracts many people.

Answer: Industrialisation

quiz.q: Which is an example of a mineral-rich area attracting population?
quiz.explain: Mining and associated industry in the copper belt attract workers.

Lesson: the Katanga-Zambia copper belt in Africa.

Answer: Katanga-Zambia copper belt
quiz.mistake: Confuses a religious centre with a mining area

quiz.q: Varanasi, Jerusalem and Vatican City attract people mainly because of:
quiz.explain: These are religious and cultural centres.

quiz.q: Industrial belts attract not only factory workers but also:
options: Transport operators, shopkeepers, bank employees, doctors and teachers
quiz.explain: Industries generate many service jobs too.
steps: Asked: who else industrial belts attract.
Lesson: transport operators, shopkeepers, bank staff, doctors and teachers.

Answer: Transport operators, shopkeepers, bank employees, doctors and teachers

quiz.q: Social and political unrest in a region usually leads to:
options: People moving out of the region
quiz.explain: Unrest is a push factor causing outmigration.
steps: Asked: the effect of social and political unrest.
Lesson: unrest pushes people out of a region.

Answer: People moving out of the region
quiz.mistake: Thinks unrest has no effect on population

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Cities attract large numbers of rural migrants. Reason (R): Cities offer better civic amenities, employment, education and medical facilities.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

steps: Check A: cities attract many rural migrants — true.

Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.q: Which of these is an economic factor influencing population distribution?
quiz.explain: Minerals, urbanisation and industrialisation are economic factors.
steps: Economic factors: minerals, urbanisation, industrialisation.

quiz.q: A new steel plant opens near an iron ore mine in a forested area. Over 20 years the area's population will most likely:

steps: A steel plant near an iron ore mine creates jobs.
Jobs attract workers and service providers, as in Jamshedpur.

Answer: Increase, as jobs attract workers and service providers

teach.nudge: Good! Mention economic factors like minerals and industry, and social or cultural ones too.

learn.hook: India added about 18 crore people between Census 2001 and 2011. How do geographers measure change on that scale?
points: Population growth (population change) is the change in the number of inhabitants of a territory over a period of time; it may be positive or negative.
Growth of population: change between two points of time in absolute numbers = later population − earlier population.
Growth rate of population: the change expressed as a percentage = (change ÷ earlier population) × 100.
Growth rate lets us compare places of very different sizes fairly.

example.q: A town had 50,000 people in 2011 and 60,000 in 2021. Find the growth and the growth rate.
example.answer: Growth = 10,000; growth rate = 20%

learn.reallife: Census 2011 showed India's decadal growth rate as 17.7% for 2001–2011, the lowest decadal growth recorded after Independence.

games.title: Growth or rate?
items: Growth of population is expressed in absolute numbers.
It is the actual difference in numbers.
Growth rate is expressed as a percentage.
Population change can never be negative.
It is negative when population falls.
Growth rate is calculated by dividing the change by the later population.

quiz.q: A district's population rose from 8,00,000 in 2011 to 9,20,000 in 2021. What is the growth of population?
quiz.explain: Growth in absolute numbers = 9,20,000 − 8,00,000 = 1,20,000.

topics.title: Natural growth, actual growth, positive and negative growth

learn.hook: Kerala has low birth rates, yet its villages fill with new houses built by Gulf migrants. Births alone don't tell the whole story.
points: Natural growth of population = births − deaths in a region between two points of time.
Actual growth of population = births − deaths + in-migration − out-migration.
Positive growth: when births exceed deaths between two points of time, or when people from other countries migrate in permanently.
Negative growth: when the population decreases between two points of time — births fall below deaths or people emigrate.

example.q: A city records 30,000 births, 10,000 deaths, 15,000 in-migrants and 5,000 out-migrants in a year. Find natural and actual growth.
example.answer: Natural growth = 20,000; actual growth = 30,000

topics.title: Births and deaths: CBR, CDR and mortality

learn.hook: Every year the Sample Registration System tells India how many babies were born per 1,000 people. That single number shapes school and hospital budgets.
points: The three components of population change are births, deaths and migration.
Crude Birth Rate (CBR) = number of live births in a year per thousand of population: CBR = (Bi ÷ P) × 1000, where Bi = live births in the year and P = mid-year population.
Crude Death Rate (CDR) = number of deaths in a year per thousand of population: CDR = (D ÷ P) × 1000.
Mortality is affected by the region's demographic structure, social advancement and levels of economic development.
Natural growth rate (per thousand) = CBR − CDR.

example.q: A town has a mid-year population of 2,00,000. In the year, 4,000 babies are born and 1,600 people die. Find CBR and CDR.
steps: Natural growth rate = 20 − 8 = 12 per thousand.
example.answer: CBR = 20, CDR = 8 per thousand

learn.reallife: India's SRS data show CBR falling to about 19.5 per thousand and CDR to about 6 per thousand in recent years — signs of demographic transition.

topics.title: Migration: types, push and pull factors

learn.hook: Every Diwali, trains from Mumbai to Patna overflow. Every harvest, Punjab's fields welcome workers from Bihar. Migration moves India.
points: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another; the place they leave is the place of origin (population falls) and the place they move to is the place of destination (population rises).
Immigrants are migrants who move into a new place; emigrants are migrants who move out of a place.
Migration may be permanent, temporary or seasonal; and rural-rural, rural-urban, urban-urban or urban-rural.
Push factors make the place of origin less attractive: unemployment, poor living conditions, political turmoil, unpleasant climate, natural disasters, epidemics and socio-economic backwardness.
Pull factors make the destination more attractive: better job opportunities and living conditions, peace and stability, security of life and property, and pleasant climate.

example.q: A farmer from drought-hit Marathwada moves to Pune for a factory job. Identify origin, destination, a push and a pull factor.
steps: Origin: Marathwada (population falls).
Destination: Pune (population rises).
Push: drought (natural disaster) and unemployment.
Pull: better job opportunities.
example.answer: Origin Marathwada, destination Pune; push = drought/unemployment; pull = jobs

learn.reallife: Seasonal migration of sugarcane cutters from Beed to western Maharashtra and Karnataka every winter is a well-known Indian case.

Answer: Security of life and property

quiz.explain: Backwardness drives people away from their place of origin.

Answer: Socio-economic backwardness
quiz.mistake: Picks an attraction at the destination

Answer: Immigrants

Answer: Decrease

Answer: Seasonal migration
quiz.mistake: Thinks any long journey is permanent

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

steps: Check A: large rural-urban migration in developing countries — true.
Check R: village unemployment pushes, city jobs pull — true.
Push and pull together cause the movement, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see push and pull as the explanation

quiz.q: A family leaves a flood-prone coastal village for a hill town with a cooler, safer climate. Which pair of factors is at work?
options: Push: pleasant climate; Pull: natural disaster

topics.title: Trends in world population growth and doubling time

learn.hook: It took more than a million years for humanity to reach 1 billion — yet only 12 years to go from 5 billion to 6 billion!
points: For most of history population grew very slowly; it was below 300 million in the first century AD.
Growth speeded up sharply after the Industrial Revolution (around 1750).
Technological advancement, expansion of world trade, better food supply and medical facilities reduced death rates, so population grew rapidly.

Doubling time — the years a population takes to double — kept shrinking: about 200 years from 1650 to 1850 (500 to 1,000 million), 80 years to 1930 (2,000 million) and 45 years to 1975 (4,000 million).
On a graph, world population looks like a 'J' curve: flat for centuries, then shooting up.

example.q: World population was 2,000 million in 1930 and 4,000 million in 1975. What was the doubling time?
steps: Doubling time = later year − earlier year when population doubled.
example.answer: 45 years

learn.reallife: Better food (Green Revolution), vaccines and clean water reduced deaths in India after 1951, causing a population 'explosion' between 1951 and 1981.

topics.title: Spatial pattern and impact of population change

learn.hook: Japan's villages have schools with no children; Niger's schools burst at the seams. Two very different population problems.
points: Spatial pattern: developed countries generally have slow (or even negative) growth; developing countries generally grow faster. Growth is negatively correlated with economic development.
A small increase in population is desirable in a growing economy; beyond a point it creates problems.
Problems of rapid growth: depletion of resources (the most serious), unemployment, and pressure on services like schools, hospitals, housing and transport.
Population decline is also a concern: it indicates that resources that supported a former population are now insufficient; it also brings ageing and a shrinking workforce.

example.q: Compare the main population problems of a fast-growing country and a shrinking one.
steps: Fast-growing: strain on resources, jobs and services.
Shrinking: ageing, fewer workers, and a sign that resources/economy no longer support the earlier population.

learn.reallife: Indian cities like Bengaluru face traffic, water and housing stress from rapid growth, while states like Kerala are already planning for an ageing population.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Is population growth good or bad? What problems come from growing too fast or shrinking?'

learn.hook: Two hundred years ago, every country had high births and high deaths. Today some have cradles empty and pensions full. The demographic transition explains the journey.
points: Demographic transition theory: population changes from high births and high deaths to low births and low deaths as society moves from rural, agrarian and illiterate to urban, industrial and literate. It helps describe and predict population.

Stage I: high fertility and high mortality, so slow growth; people mostly in agriculture, large families, low life expectancy, mostly illiterate, low technology. About 200 years ago all countries were in this stage.
Stage II: fertility remains high at first and declines with time; mortality falls due to better sanitation and health — the gap between births and deaths causes a large increase in population.
Stage III: both fertility and mortality decline considerably; population is stable or grows slowly; society is urbanised, literate, with high technical know-how and deliberately controls family size.

On the diagram, the birth-rate and death-rate curves start high, the death-rate curve falls first, the birth-rate curve falls later; total population rises steeply in the gap. Countries today are at different stages.

example.q: A country has a birth rate of 38 and a death rate of 12 per thousand, with death rates falling fast due to new hospitals. Which stage is it in?
steps: High birth rate still (38).
Death rate already falling (12).
Large gap → rapid growth.
This matches Stage II.
example.answer: Stage II

learn.reallife: India moved from Stage II (high births, falling deaths after 1951) towards Stage III, with total fertility rate now at about 2.0 (NFHS-5) — below replacement level.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Population grows slowly in Stage III. Reason (R): Both fertility and mortality have declined considerably.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

quiz.explain: Both true; with both rates low, the gap is small and growth slow.
steps: Check A: growth is slow in Stage III — true.
Check R: both fertility and mortality have declined considerably — true.
With both low, the gap is small, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks low death rate always means fast growth

quiz.q: A country has CBR 15 and CDR 8 per thousand, high literacy and mostly urban living. Its natural growth rate and likely stage are:

Answer: 7 per thousand; Stage III

revise.summary: Demographic transition theory says population moves from high births and high deaths to low births and low deaths as society becomes urban, industrial and literate. Growth is slow in Stage I, fastest in Stage II (deaths fall first), and slow again in Stage III.

Reading the diagram: death rate falls first

Stage II: fertility high then declining; mortality falls (sanitation, health) → large increase
Stage III: both low; slow or stable growth; urban, literate, family size controlled
traps: High births alone do not mean fast growth — in Stage I high deaths cancel them

learn.hook: In 1798 an English clergyman predicted that people would outgrow food and face famine. Was Thomas Malthus right?
points: Family planning is the spacing or preventing of the birth of children; access to family planning services helps limit population growth and improves women's health.
Government measures include propaganda (awareness campaigns), free availability of contraceptives and tax disincentives for large families.
Thomas Malthus (1798): the number of people would increase faster than the food supply; any further increase would result in a population crash caused by famine, disease and war.
Malthus' natural (physical) checks are famine, disease and war; preventive checks (like late marriage and self-restraint) are better than physical checks.
Exam focus: distribution factors, positive vs negative growth, CBR/CDR numericals and stages of demographic transition.

example.q: Classify Malthus' checks: delayed marriage, famine, epidemic, self-restraint, war.
steps: Natural/physical checks occur through suffering: famine, epidemic (disease), war.
Preventive checks are chosen by people: delayed marriage, self-restraint.
example.answer: Natural checks: famine, epidemic, war; preventive checks: delayed marriage, self-restraint

learn.reallife: India launched the world's first national family planning programme in 1952; schemes like Mission Parivar Vikas promote access to contraceptives in high-fertility districts.

learn.hook: A city's GDP doubles, but its rivers turn black and its children still skip school. Has it grown or developed?
points: Both growth and development refer to changes over a period of time.
Growth is quantitative and value neutral: it may be positive (increase) or negative (decrease).
Development means a qualitative change and is always value positive; development occurs when there is positive growth plus a positive change in quality.
For a long time, a country's development was measured only by economic growth (GNP, per capita income): a bigger economy was assumed to mean a more developed country.
Paradox: a country can show high economic growth while most of its people still lack good health, education and choices.

example.q: A town's population rises from 50,000 to 70,000, but traffic, slums and pollution worsen. Is this growth, development or both?
steps: Population increased — a quantitative change, so growth (positive).
Quality of life worsened, so there is no positive qualitative change.
Hence growth without development.
example.answer: Growth, but not development

learn.reallife: India's GDP grew fast after 1991, yet NFHS surveys showed high child stunting — a reminder that growth alone does not guarantee development.

topics.title: The concept of human development: Haq and Sen

learn.hook: A Pakistani economist and an Indian economist, friends from college, changed how the world measures progress.
points: The concept of human development was introduced by Dr Mahbub-ul-Haq, a Pakistani economist: development should enlarge people's choices and improve their lives; people are central to all development.

Prof. Amartya Sen saw an increase in freedom (or decrease in unfreedom) as the main objective of development; social and political institutions and processes play an important role in increasing freedom.
The Human Development Report has been published annually by the UNDP since 1990.
The most important aspects: leading a long and healthy life, being able to gain knowledge, and having enough means to live a decent life.
Hence access to resources, health and education are the key areas; lack of these capabilities limits people's choices.

example.q: Why does lack of education limit a person's choices, according to the human development concept?
steps: Human development is about enlarging choices.
Choices need capabilities — health, knowledge and resources.
Without education, a person cannot access many jobs or information, so choices shrink.
example.answer: Without knowledge (a key capability), people's choices narrow

learn.reallife: Kerala's investment in schools and health clinics has long given it top human development indicators in India, showing Haq's idea of putting people first.

topics.title: Pillars of human development: equity and sustainability

learn.hook: Imagine a house on four pillars. Remove one, and the roof tilts. Human development stands on four such pillars.
points: The four pillars of human development are equity, sustainability, productivity and empowerment.
Equity: making equal access to opportunities available to everybody, irrespective of gender, race, income and, in the Indian case, caste.
Example: in India, a large number of women and persons from socially and economically backward groups drop out of school — this shows how access to knowledge is limited by unequal opportunity.
Sustainability: continuity in the availability of opportunities; each generation must have the same opportunities. Misuse of environmental, financial and human resources reduces future options.
Example: if a community does not stress sending girls to school, many opportunities are lost to these young women when they grow up.

example.q: A village over-pumps groundwater for paddy, leaving dry wells for the next generation. Which pillar is violated?
steps: The issue is about future availability of a resource.
Future generations will have fewer opportunities.
That breaks sustainability.
example.answer: Sustainability

learn.reallife: Schemes like Beti Bachao Beti Padhao and scholarships for SC/ST students try to strengthen equity in education.

topics.title: Pillars of human development: productivity and empowerment

learn.hook: A worker who is healthy and skilled produces more. A woman who can decide for herself shapes her family's future. Two more pillars!
points: Productivity means human labour productivity, or productivity in terms of human work; it must be constantly enriched by building capabilities in people.
Efforts to increase knowledge or provide better health facilities lead to better work efficiency — people are the real wealth of nations.
Empowerment means having the power to make choices; it comes from increasing freedom and capability.
Good governance and people-oriented policies are required to empower people; empowerment of socially and economically disadvantaged groups is of special importance.

learn.hook: Is development about more money, more welfare schemes, basic needs, or building abilities? Four approaches, four answers.
points: Income approach: one of the oldest; human development is linked to income; the level of income reflects the level of freedom an individual enjoys — higher income, higher development.

Welfare approach: looks at human beings as beneficiaries or targets of development activities; argues for higher government expenditure on education, health, social security and amenities; people are passive recipients, not participants.

Basic needs approach: initially proposed by the International Labour Organisation (ILO); six basic needs — health, education, food, water supply, sanitation and housing; the question of human choices is ignored; the emphasis is on providing basic needs to defined sections.
Capability approach: associated with Prof. Amartya Sen; building human capabilities in health, education and access to resources is the key to increasing human development.

steps: The scheme supplies items from the list of basic needs (food, housing) to a defined group.
People's own choices and abilities are not considered.
Providing basic needs while ignoring choices is the basic needs approach.
example.answer: Basic needs approach

learn.reallife: PM Awas Yojana (housing) and Jal Jeevan Mission (tap water) meet basic needs, while Skill India builds capabilities — India uses a mix of approaches.

learn.hook: One number between 0 and 1 that sums up a nation's health, learning and living standard. That's the HDI.
points: The Human Development Index (HDI) ranks countries based on their performance in health, education and access to resources; scores range from 0 to 1 — the closer to 1, the higher the human development.
Health indicator: life expectancy at birth — a longer life expectancy means a greater chance of a long and healthy life.
Education indicator: earlier, adult literacy rate and gross enrolment ratio; now measured by mean years of schooling and expected years of schooling.
Access to resources: measured in terms of purchasing power (in US dollars), i.e. GNI per capita (PPP).
Each dimension gets a weightage of 1/3; in NCERT's simple description, the HDI is the sum of the weights assigned to all three dimensions.

topics.title: Human Poverty Index and Gross National Happiness

learn.hook: HDI tells you how far a country has come. Another index asks: how many are still left behind? And Bhutan asks: are people happy?
points: HDI measures attainment (what has been achieved); the Human Poverty Index (HPI) measures shortfall (what is still lacking).
HPI is a non-income measure using: probability of not surviving till age 40, adult illiteracy rate, number of people without access to clean water, and number of small children who are underweight.
Gross National Happiness (GNH): Bhutan officially measures progress by happiness; it stresses spiritual, non-material and qualitative aspects of well-being.
These measures remind us that development is more than income — material progress should not come at the cost of the environment, culture or spiritual life.

example.q: Two countries have the same HDI. Country A has 30% underweight children; B has 10%. Which index would show the difference, and how?
steps: HDI shows the same attainment for both.

example.answer: The HPI would show greater shortfall (poverty) in Country A

learn.hook: Sri Lanka ranks above India in human development though its economy is far smaller. Size isn't everything!
points: Size of territory and per capita income are not directly related to human development; small countries often do better than large ones, and relatively poorer nations can rank higher than richer neighbours.
Countries are grouped by HDI score: very high (0.800 and above), high (0.700–0.799), medium (0.550–0.699) and low (below 0.550).
Very high and high HDI countries invest more in the social sector and are generally free of political turmoil; examples include Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Australia.
Medium HDI countries mostly emerged after the colonial period (after World War II); many are trying to become more people-oriented; India is in this group.
Low HDI countries are mostly small countries going through political turmoil and social instability — civil war, famine or high incidence of diseases; many are in sub-Saharan Africa.

example.answer: Very high, high, medium, low

learn.hook: Why do some poorer countries beat richer ones in HDI? Look at how they spend and how they govern.
points: Good governance and higher spending on the social sector (education, health, water, sanitation) raise human development faster than income growth alone.
A world map of HDI shows very high HDI in North America, Europe, Australia, New Zealand and Japan; low HDI concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa.
Tables of the top and bottom countries help compare: European nations dominate the top, while several African countries fill the bottom ranks.
Exam focus: pillars and approaches (MCQs), growth vs development, the four pillars, key areas of human development, and HDI categories with their characteristics.

example.q: Two states have equal income per head. State A spends 30% of its budget on health and education; state B spends 12%. Which will likely have higher human development, and why?
steps: Income is equal, so the difference comes from spending.
A invests more in the social sector.
Better health and education raise HDI indicators.
example.answer: State A, because of greater social sector investment

learn.reallife: Kerala, with moderate per capita income but high spending on health and schooling, has long topped Indian states in human development.

games.title: Where on the HDI map?
items: Sahel countries like Niger and Chad

games.title: Governance matters
items: Social sector spending can raise human development even without very high income.
All African countries have very high HDI.
Many sub-Saharan countries are in the low group.
Political stability helps raise human development.
Governance has no effect on human development.
Good governance is a key factor.

quiz.q: Which region has the largest concentration of low HDI countries?
quiz.explain: Most low HDI countries are in sub-Saharan Africa.
steps: Lesson: low HDI is concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa.
Europe, North America and Australia are very high.
So the answer is sub-Saharan Africa.
Answer: Sub-Saharan Africa

quiz.q: Which factor most explains why a country with moderate income can achieve high human development?
options: High investment in the social sector and good governance
quiz.explain: Spending on health and education and good governance improve HDI.
steps: Lesson: good governance and higher social-sector spending raise human development faster than income alone.
Area, population and army size do not raise HDI.
So the answer is social investment and good governance.
Answer: High investment in the social sector and good governance
quiz.mistake: Thinks area or population raise HDI

quiz.q: Which pair of pillars of human development is correctly described?
options: Equity — future generations; Empowerment — labour output
Equity — equal access; Empowerment — power to make choices
quiz.explain: Equity is equal access; empowerment is the power to make choices.
steps: Equity = equal access; empowerment = power to make choices.
The other pairs swap or invent meanings.
Answer: Equity — equal access; Empowerment — power to make choices

quiz.q: Which of the following best explains 'key areas of human development'?
options: Health, education and access to resources
quiz.explain: These three key areas define human development.
steps: Lesson: the key areas are health, education and access to resources.
Industry, trade or transport are economic sectors, not these areas.
So the answer is health, education and access to resources.
Answer: Health, education and access to resources

quiz.q: On a world HDI map, Japan would be shown in which category?
quiz.explain: Japan is in the very high human development group.
steps: Lesson: very high HDI includes North America, Europe, Australia, New Zealand and Japan.
So Japan is in the very high category.
Answer: Very high
quiz.mistake: Assumes Asian countries are all medium

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Low HDI countries often face civil war and famine. Reason (R): Political turmoil and social instability reduce investment in health and education.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; instability diverts resources from the social sector, keeping HDI low.
steps: Check A: low HDI countries often face civil war and famine — true.
Check R: turmoil and instability reduce investment in health and education — true.
Less social investment keeps HDI low, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not link instability to low social investment

quiz.q: A question asks you to 'differentiate between growth and development'. Which pair of points is most relevant?
options: Quantitative and value neutral vs qualitative and value positive
quiz.explain: That is the core distinction.
steps: The core distinction: growth is quantitative and value neutral.
Development is qualitative and value positive.
Answer: Quantitative and value neutral vs qualitative and value positive

quiz.q: A country spends little on schools and clinics, faces frequent coups and has a falling life expectancy. Its HDI category is most likely:
quiz.explain: Political turmoil and poor social spending typify low HDI countries.
steps: Clues: little spending on schools and clinics, frequent coups, falling life expectancy.
Lesson: political turmoil and poor social spending mark low HDI countries.
So the most likely category is low.
Answer: Low

teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! Spend on people, govern well, keep peace — and HDI rises!
teach.nudge: Good! Mention social sector spending and governance or political stability.

revise.summary: Good governance and higher social-sector spending raise human development faster than income growth alone. Very high HDI is found in North America, Europe, Australia, New Zealand and Japan, while low HDI is concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa.

Revising pillars, approaches and the growth–development distinction

learn.hook: A coal miner in Jharia, a fisherwoman in Kerala and a wheat farmer in Punjab share one thing: they earn directly from the earth.
points: Human economic activities are grouped as primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary and quinary.

Primary activities depend directly on the environment and use earth's resources like land, water, vegetation, building materials and minerals: hunting, gathering, pastoral activities, fishing, forestry, agriculture, and mining and quarrying.
People engaged in primary activities are called red-collar workers because of the outdoor nature of their work.
As an economy develops, the share of its workforce in primary activities falls and more people move to secondary and tertiary work.

example.q: Classify: (a) a quarry worker in Rajasthan, (b) a textile mill worker in Surat, (c) a bank clerk in Kolkata.
steps: (a) Quarrying uses earth's resources directly → primary.
(b) Turning cotton into cloth → secondary.
(c) Providing a service → tertiary.
example.answer: (a) primary, (b) secondary, (c) tertiary

learn.reallife: Over 40% of India's workforce is still in agriculture (PLFS), while in the USA it is under 2% — a clear sign of different development levels.

games.title: Red-collar facts
items: Primary activity workers are called red-collar workers.
Mining and quarrying are primary activities.
They extract resources directly from the earth.
The share of workers in primary activities rises as economies develop.

quiz.q: People engaged in primary activities are called:
quiz.explain: Their outdoor work earns them the name red-collar workers.
steps: Asked: the name for primary workers.
Lesson: they are called red-collar workers because of their outdoor work.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a primary activity?
quiz.explain: Manufacturing transforms raw materials — a secondary activity.
steps: Primary activities extract resources directly: hunting, mining, pastoralism and others.
Manufacturing turns raw materials into goods — a secondary activity.
So manufacturing is NOT primary.
Answer: Manufacturing

quiz.q: Primary activities are those that:
quiz.explain: They use earth's resources directly.
steps: Lesson: primary activities depend directly on the environment.
Services are tertiary and factory processing is secondary.
So the answer is depending directly on the environment.
Answer: Depend directly on the environment

quiz.q: Why are primary activity workers called red-collar workers?
options: Because they work in research labs
Because of the outdoor nature of their work
quiz.explain: The name reflects working outdoors in sun and soil.
steps: Lesson: the name comes from the outdoor nature of their work.
It has nothing to do with uniform colour.
So the answer is the outdoor nature of their work.
Answer: Because of the outdoor nature of their work

quiz.q: As a country's economy develops, the proportion of workers in primary activities generally:
quiz.explain: Workers shift to secondary and tertiary sectors with development.
steps: Lesson: as an economy develops, the primary share of the workforce falls.
Workers move to secondary and tertiary work.
So it decreases.
Answer: Decreases

quiz.q: Which list contains only primary activities?
quiz.explain: Gathering, fishing and quarrying all extract resources directly.
steps: Check each list: gathering, fishing, quarrying all extract resources directly.
Banking, steel-making, teaching and trade are not primary.
So only 'Gathering, fishing, quarrying' is all primary.
Answer: Gathering, fishing, quarrying

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Agriculture is a primary activity. Reason (R): It depends directly on land, water and climate.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; direct dependence on environmental resources is what makes it primary.
steps: Check A: agriculture is a primary activity — true.
Check R: it depends directly on land, water and climate — true.
Direct dependence on nature is what makes it primary, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks agriculture is secondary because it produces goods

quiz.q: Assertion (A): In highly developed economies, most workers are in primary activities. Reason (R): As economies develop, workers shift from primary to secondary and tertiary activities.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: developed economies have only a small share in primary work. R is true.
steps: Check A: most workers in developed economies are in primary work — false.
Check R: development shifts workers to secondary and tertiary — true.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true

revise.summary: Economic activities are primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary and quinary. Primary activities depend directly on the environment — hunting, gathering, pastoralism, fishing, forestry, agriculture, mining — and their workers are called red-collar workers; their share falls as an economy develops.

learn.hook: Ever chewed gum? Its original base, chicle, was gathered from the sap of the Zapota tree in Central America.
points: The earliest humans depended on their immediate environment for food, shelter and clothing; hunting and gathering are the oldest economic activities.
Early hunters used primitive tools made of stones, twigs or arrows; people near coasts also fished.

Gathering is practised in high latitudes (northern Canada, northern Eurasia, southern Chile) and low latitudes (Amazon basin, tropical Africa, northern fringe of Australia and interior parts of South-east Asia).

Modern gathering is market-oriented: bark for quinine, tannin extract and cork; leaves for beverages, drugs and cosmetics; fibres for thatch and cloth; nuts for food and oils; tree trunks for rubber, balata, gums and resins. Chicle from Zapota tree milk makes chewing gum.
Gathering needs little capital and low technology; yield per person is very low and little or no surplus is produced.

example.q: Why is gathering unlikely to be important in the global economy?
steps: It uses very low technology and little capital.
Yield per person is low and there is hardly any surplus to sell.
Synthetic substitutes of better quality and lower price have replaced many gathered products.
example.answer: Low yield, no surplus and competition from synthetic products

learn.reallife: Tribal communities in Jharkhand and Odisha collect tendu leaves, mahua and sal seeds; cooperatives like TRIFED help them sell these forest products.

games.title: High or low latitude gathering zone?

quiz.q: Chicle, used for making chewing gum, is obtained from:
options: The bark of the cinchona tree
The milk of the Zapota tree
quiz.explain: Chicle is made from the milky sap of the Zapota tree.
steps: Asked: source of chicle for chewing gum.
Lesson: chicle comes from the milk of the Zapota tree.
Quinine comes from bark, so the cinchona option is wrong.
Answer: The milk of the Zapota tree

quiz.q: Which of these is a high-latitude zone of gathering?
quiz.explain: Northern Canada, northern Eurasia and southern Chile are high-latitude gathering zones.
steps: High-latitude gathering zones: northern Canada, northern Eurasia, southern Chile.
Amazon, tropical Africa and South-east Asia are low-latitude zones.
So the answer is northern Canada.
Answer: Northern Canada

quiz.q: Which is NOT a feature of gathering?
quiz.explain: Gathering produces little or no surplus.
steps: Lesson: gathering has low capital, low technology and low yield per person.
It produces little or no surplus.
So 'large surplus for trade' is NOT a feature.
Answer: Large surplus for trade

quiz.q: Bark of trees gathered in modern times is used for:
quiz.explain: Bark yields quinine, tannin and cork; fibres give thatch and cloth.
steps: Lesson: bark is used for quinine, tannin extract and cork.
Fibres give thatch and cloth; leaves give beverages and cosmetics.
So the answer is quinine, tannin extract and cork.
Answer: Quinine, tannin extract and cork

quiz.q: Early hunters made their tools from:
quiz.explain: Primitive tools were made of natural materials.
steps: Lesson: early hunters used primitive tools of stones, twigs or arrows.
Metals and plastic came much later.
So the answer is stones, twigs or arrows.
Answer: Stones, twigs or arrows
quiz.mistake: Assumes metals were used from the start

quiz.q: On a world map of subsistence gathering, which region would be marked?
quiz.explain: The Amazon basin is a major low-latitude gathering zone.
steps: Low-latitude gathering zones include the Amazon basin.
The Corn Belt, Paris basin and Great Lakes are farming or industrial regions.
So the Amazon basin would be marked.
Answer: Amazon basin

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Gathering is unlikely to become important at the global level. Reason (R): Many gathered products face competition from cheaper and better-quality synthetic substitutes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; synthetic products have replaced many gathered ones, limiting gathering's global role.
steps: Check A: gathering will not become globally important — true.
Check R: cheaper, better synthetic substitutes compete — true.
Substitutes replacing gathered goods limit it, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Gatherers today often sell valuable plant products in markets. Reason (R): Modern gathering is purely for self-consumption.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: modern gathering is partly market-oriented.
steps: Check A: gatherers sell valuable plant products in markets — true.
Check R: 'purely for self-consumption' — false; modern gathering is market-oriented.
So A is true, but R is false.

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Where is gathering still practised, and what do gatherers collect today?'

revise.summary: Hunting and gathering are the oldest economic activities, using primitive tools and the immediate environment. Gathering survives in high and low latitudes, and modern gathering is partly market-oriented, but low yield, no surplus and synthetic substitutes limit it.

Plant parts gathered and their products (bark, leaves, fibres, nuts, trunks)

learn.hook: Every summer, Gaddi shepherds in Himachal drive thousands of sheep up to high meadows; every winter they bring them down. This ancient rhythm has a name — transhumance.
points: After hunting, people learned to domesticate animals; pastoralism may be subsistence (nomadic herding) or commercial (livestock rearing).

Nomadic herding or pastoral nomadism is a primitive subsistence activity: herders depend on animals for food, clothing, shelter, tools and transport, moving with their livestock for pasture and water.
Animals vary by region: cattle in tropical Africa; sheep, goats and camels in the Sahara and Asiatic deserts; yak in Tibet; llamas in the Andes; reindeer in the Arctic and sub-Arctic.

Three main regions: (1) the core region from the Atlantic shores of North Africa eastwards across the Arabian peninsula into Mongolia and Central China; (2) the tundra region of Eurasia; (3) South-west Africa and the island of Madagascar.

Transhumance: seasonal migration from plains to mountain pastures in summer and back to the plains in winter — e.g. Gujjars, Bakarwals, Gaddis and Bhotiyas in the Himalayas. Pastoral nomadism is declining due to political boundaries and new settlement plans.

example.q: A Bakarwal family in Jammu moves its goats to the high pastures of Kashmir in April and returns in October. Explain the movement.
steps: Summer: plains get hot and dry; mountain pastures are green → move up.
Winter: mountains get snow-covered → move down.
This seasonal vertical movement is transhumance.
example.answer: Transhumance (seasonal vertical migration)

learn.reallife: Raika camel herders of Rajasthan and Gaddi shepherds of Himachal still practise pastoralism, though grazing land is shrinking.

games.title: Herder truths
items: Transhumance means moving to mountain pastures in summer and back to plains in winter.

Nomadic herding is a highly capital-intensive commercial activity.
It is a primitive subsistence activity.
The tundra region of Eurasia is one of the main regions of nomadic herding.
It is the second major region.
Political boundaries have helped pastoral nomadism expand.
Boundaries and settlement plans have caused its decline.

quiz.q: Which animal is most important for nomadic herders in the Arctic and sub-Arctic regions?

quiz.q: Llamas are the main herded animals in the:

Yaks are herded in Tibet.

The Pampas of Argentina is not one of them.
It is an extensive grain and commercial livestock region.
Answer: Pampas of Argentina

quiz.q: Gujjars, Bakarwals, Gaddis and Bhotiyas are examples of communities practising:
quiz.explain: They migrate seasonally between plains and Himalayan pastures.
steps: Gujjars, Bakarwals, Gaddis, Bhotiyas move seasonally between plains and Himalayan pastures.

quiz.q: In transhumance in the Himalayas, herders move to the mountains in:
quiz.explain: In summer they go up to high pastures; in winter they come down.
steps: Lesson: herders move up to mountain pastures in summer.
They return to the plains in winter.

quiz.q: In tundra regions, nomadic herders move:
options: North to south in summer, south to north in winter
South to north in summer, north to south in winter
quiz.explain: They follow the summer thaw northwards and retreat south in winter.
steps: In tundra regions, summer thaw opens pastures in the north.
Herders move south to north in summer and north to south in winter.
Answer: South to north in summer, north to south in winter

quiz.q: Pastoral nomadism has declined mainly because of:
options: Imposition of political boundaries and new settlement plans
quiz.explain: Borders and government settlement schemes restrict free movement.
steps: Lesson: pastoral nomadism is declining due to political boundaries and new settlement plans.
More pasture would help nomadism, not reduce it.
So the answer is political boundaries and settlement plans.
Answer: Imposition of political boundaries and new settlement plans
quiz.mistake: Picks a factor that would help nomadism

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Pastoral nomads depend on animals for food, clothing, shelter, tools and transport. Reason (R): Nomadic herding is a primitive subsistence activity.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; being a subsistence activity, herders meet almost all their needs from their animals.
steps: Check A: nomads depend on animals for food, clothing, shelter, tools and transport — true.
Check R: nomadic herding is a primitive subsistence activity — true.
Being subsistence-based, herders meet their needs from animals, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see subsistence as the explanation

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'What is nomadic herding? Where is it practised and what is transhumance?'
teach.praise: Tweet-tweet! Herders move with their animals, and transhumance is the seasonal up-and-down trip!
teach.nudge: Good! Explain transhumance and name at least one main region of nomadic herding.

revise.summary: Pastoralism may be subsistence (nomadic herding) or commercial. Nomads depend on animals for almost all needs and move for pasture and water in three main regions; transhumance is seasonal movement up to mountain pastures in summer and down in winter.
focus: Matching herded animals to regions
The three main regions of nomadic herding
Transhumance and Himalayan communities; causes of decline
remember: Cattle — tropical Africa; sheep, goats, camels — Sahara and Asiatic deserts; yak — Tibet; llama — Andes; reindeer — Arctic and sub-Arctic
Regions: North Africa to Mongolia and Central China; tundra of Eurasia; South-west Africa and Madagascar

learn.hook: New Zealand has about five sheep for every person! Its fenced ranches export wool and meat worldwide.
points: Commercial livestock rearing is more organised and capital intensive than nomadic herding; it is associated with western cultures and practised on permanent ranches.

Ranches cover large areas divided into parcels fenced to regulate grazing; when one parcel is grazed, animals move to another (rotational grazing). The number of animals is kept within the pasture's carrying capacity.
It is a specialised activity rearing one type of animal — sheep, cattle, goats or horses; meat, wool, hides and skin are processed and packed scientifically and exported to world markets.
Emphasis on breeding, genetic improvement, disease control and health care.
Important countries: New Zealand, Australia, Argentina, Uruguay and the USA.

example.q: Give three differences between nomadic herding and commercial livestock rearing.
steps: Nomadic: subsistence, moving herds; commercial: market-oriented, permanent ranches.
Nomadic: many types of animals kept; commercial: one type of animal (specialised).
Nomadic: little capital or science; commercial: capital intensive with scientific breeding and disease control.
example.answer: Subsistence vs commercial; mixed vs single animal; low vs high capital and science

learn.reallife: India's dairy and poultry giants use scientific breeding and veterinary care, borrowing practices from commercial livestock rearing.

items.text: Ranches are divided into fenced ___ to regulate grazing.
The number of animals is kept according to the ___ capacity of the pasture.

quiz.q: Commercial livestock rearing is practised on:
quiz.explain: It is organised on large, permanent ranches.
steps: Lesson: commercial livestock rearing is practised on permanent ranches.

quiz.q: Why are ranches divided into fenced parcels?

When one parcel is grazed, animals move to another.

quiz.q: Which practice is emphasised in commercial livestock rearing?

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Commercial livestock rearing is capital intensive. Reason (R): It needs fencing, scientific breeding, veterinary care and processing facilities.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; these costly inputs are why it is capital intensive.
steps: Check A: commercial rearing is capital intensive — true.
Check R: it needs fencing, breeding, veterinary care, processing — true.
These costly inputs make it capital intensive, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Commercial livestock rearing is associated mainly with subsistence cultures. Reason (R): Its products are processed, packed and exported to world markets.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: it is associated with western commercial cultures. R is true.
steps: Check A: associated mainly with subsistence cultures — false; it is linked with western cultures.
Check R: products are processed and exported — true.

learn.hook: In Mizoram's hills, smoke rises from burning forest patches in March. It's not a wildfire — it's jhum cultivation.
points: Agriculture is practised under many combinations of physical and socio-economic conditions, giving different farming systems.
Subsistence agriculture: the farming area consumes all, or nearly all, of the produce grown locally. It has two types: primitive and intensive.
Primitive subsistence agriculture or shifting cultivation is practised by many tribes in the tropics, especially in Africa, South and Central America and South-east Asia.

Vegetation is cleared by fire and ashes add to soil fertility (slash and burn); patches are small and tools primitive (sticks, hoes); after 3 to 5 years the soil loses fertility and the farmer shifts. The jhum cycle shortens as fertility falls and population grows.
Regional names: Jhuming in north-eastern India, Milpa in Central America and Mexico, Ladang in Indonesia and Malaysia.

example.q: A farmer clears a hill patch by fire, grows rice and maize for 4 years, then moves to a new patch. What are the advantages and problems?
steps: Advantage: ash fertilises soil, little capital needed.

Problem: as population grows, fallow periods shorten, causing deforestation and soil erosion.
example.answer: Cheap and simple, but leads to short fallow cycles, deforestation and soil erosion

learn.hook: A family in West Bengal grows two or three crops a year on less than one hectare. How can tiny farms feed so many?
points: Intensive subsistence agriculture is found in the densely populated regions of monsoon Asia.

Type 1 — dominated by wet paddy: very small holdings due to high population density; family labour; intensive use of land; little machinery; farmyard manure maintains fertility. Yield per unit area is high but labour productivity is low.

Type 2 — dominated by crops other than paddy: where relief, climate or soil do not suit paddy, crops like wheat, soyabean, barley and sorghum are grown in northern China, Manchuria, North Korea and North Japan; irrigation is used.
In India, wheat is grown in the western Indo-Gangetic plains and millets in drier parts of western and southern India under this system.

learn.hook: Assam's tea gardens began under British planters in the 1830s. Today, a cup of Assam tea is drunk across the world.

topics.title: Market gardening, truck farming and factory farming

learn.hook: Tulips cut in the Netherlands in the morning sit in flower shops in Paris, London and Berlin by evening. Welcome to market gardening!
points: Market gardening and horticulture specialise in high-value crops — vegetables, fruits and flowers — solely for urban markets.

Farms are small and located where there are good transport links to urban centres with high-income consumers; it is both labour and capital intensive, using irrigation, HYV seeds, fertilisers, insecticides, greenhouses and artificial heating in colder regions.

Well developed in densely populated industrial districts of north-west Europe, north-eastern USA and the Mediterranean; the Netherlands specialises in flowers and horticultural crops, especially tulips, flown to major European cities.
Truck farming: where farmers specialise in vegetables only; the distance of truck farms from the market is governed by the distance a truck can cover overnight.

Factory farming: a modern development in industrial regions of Western Europe and North America; poultry and cattle reared in stalls and pens, fed on manufactured feedstuff, supervised against disease; needs heavy capital for buildings, machinery, veterinary services, heating and lighting, with breed selection and scientific breeding.
