learn.hook: Between 1950–51 and 2014–15, India's land under roads, towns and factories grew fastest of all. Which categories shrank?
points: Four categories increased: forest, land under non-agricultural uses, current fallow and net area sown.
Four categories declined: barren and wasteland, culturable wasteland, area under pastures and tree crops, and fallow lands other than current fallow.

Reasons: the rate of increase is highest for non-agricultural uses due to the changing structure of the economy (industry, services), infrastructure and expansion of settlements; forest area rose mainly due to more demarcated area, not an actual increase in forest cover; current fallow fluctuates with rainfall and cropping cycles; net area sown increased recently due to use of culturable wasteland for agriculture.
Barren and wastelands declined as pressure on land brought them into use; pastures declined due to pressure from agricultural land and illegal encroachment by expanding cultivation.
In a bar graph of shares, compare the height of each category's bar in 1950–51 and 2014–15 to see increase or decline.

example.answer: Increased: forest, non-agricultural uses; declined: culturable wasteland, pastures

topics.title: Agricultural land use and cropping intensity

learn.hook: India can't create new land — so how can it grow more food? By growing more crops on the same field each year.
points: Land is more crucial for people who depend on agriculture than for those in other sectors: agriculture is purely land-based, and the quality of land directly affects productivity.
In rural areas, land ownership has social value and acts as security for credit, natural hazards and life contingencies; landlessness is closely linked with poverty.
Total stock of agricultural land = net sown area + all fallow lands + culturable wasteland.
The scope for bringing more land under cultivation is very limited, as most cultivable land is already in use; so India must raise output from existing land.
This means increasing cropping intensity and productivity. Cropping intensity (%) = (gross cropped area ÷ net sown area) × 100.

example.q: A district has a net sown area of 2,00,000 ha and a gross cropped area of 3,00,000 ha. Find its cropping intensity.
steps: Cropping intensity = GCA ÷ NSA × 100.

topics.title: Cropping seasons: kharif, rabi and zaid

learn.hook: Paddy transplanting begins with the June monsoon; wheat sowing waits for October's cool; watermelons ripen in May's heat. India farms in three seasons.
points: India has three distinct cropping seasons in the northern and interior parts: kharif, rabi and zaid.

Kharif largely coincides with the south-west monsoon and supports tropical crops: rice, cotton, jute, jowar, bajra and tur (in the north: rice, cotton, bajra, maize, jowar, tur; in the south: rice, maize, ragi, jowar, groundnut).

Rabi begins with the onset of winter in October–November and ends in March–April; low temperatures favour temperate and subtropical crops: wheat, gram, mustard (north: wheat, gram, rapeseed and mustard, barley; south: rice, maize, ragi, groundnut, jowar).
Zaid is a short-duration summer season after the rabi harvest: watermelons, cucumbers, vegetables and fodder crops on irrigated lands (south: rice, vegetables, fodder).
This distinction does not exist in southern parts: temperatures are high enough to grow tropical crops in any period if soil moisture is available.

example.q: Assign the season: (a) wheat in Punjab; (b) jute in West Bengal; (c) watermelon in Uttar Pradesh in May.
steps: (a) Sown Oct–Nov, harvested Mar–Apr → rabi.
(b) Grown with the south-west monsoon → kharif.
(c) Short summer crop after rabi, irrigated → zaid.
example.answer: (a) rabi, (b) kharif, (c) zaid

topics.title: Types of farming: irrigated and rainfed

learn.hook: Ragi in Karnataka's dry uplands and rice in Kerala's waterlogged fields — both are rainfed. One is dryland farming, the other wetland!
points: By main source of moisture, farming is irrigated or rainfed (barani).

Irrigated farming: protective irrigation protects crops from soil moisture deficiency, acting as a supplement to rainfall; productive irrigation provides sufficient soil moisture to achieve high productivity — its water input per unit area is higher.

Rainfed farming is of two types: dryland farming, largely in regions with annual rainfall below 75 cm, growing hardy, drought-resistant crops like ragi, bajra, moong, gram and guar (fodder), with soil moisture conservation and rainwater harvesting.

Wetland farming: rainfall exceeds the soil moisture requirement of plants in the rainy season; such regions may face floods and soil erosion; they grow water-intensive crops such as rice, jute and sugarcane and practise aquaculture in fresh water bodies.
Map reading: compare a rainfall map with an irrigation map — low-rainfall areas with little irrigation practise dryland farming; high-rainfall areas practise wetland farming.

learn.hook: In West Bengal, farmers grow rice three times a year and give each crop a name: aus, aman and boro.
points: Foodgrains — cereals and pulses — dominate India's cropping pattern. Cereals are classified as fine grains (rice, wheat) and coarse grains (jowar, bajra, maize, ragi etc.).

Rice is the staple food for most Indians; NCERT (2016 data) ranks India second after China; recent estimates (2024–25) put India marginally ahead. It is grown from humid tropics to the hills; in West Bengal three crops — aus, aman and boro — are grown, while in the Himalayas and north-west it is a kharif crop.

Leading rice producers: West Bengal, Punjab and Uttar Pradesh; yields are high in Punjab, Tamil Nadu, Haryana, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, West Bengal and Kerala. Rice is rainfed in many humid areas; in Punjab and Haryana it is grown under irrigation.

Wheat is the second most important cereal; being a temperate crop, it is grown in the rabi season, mostly under irrigation. About 85% of its area is in the north and central regions — Indo-Gangetic plain, Malwa plateau and Himalayas up to 2,700 m.
Leading wheat producers: Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh; yields are very high in Punjab and Haryana.

example.q: Why is wheat a rabi crop in India while rice is mostly a kharif crop?
steps: Wheat is a temperate crop needing cool weather → grown in winter (rabi).
Rice is a tropical crop needing heat and water → grown with the monsoon (kharif).
Season matches each crop's climatic needs.
example.answer: Wheat needs cool winters; rice needs monsoon heat and water

learn.hook: Dal-chawal on your plate and mustard oil in the kitchen — pulses and oilseeds fuel India's kitchens and fix nitrogen in its soils.

topics.title: Fibre and other crops: cotton, jute, sugarcane, tea and coffee

learn.hook: Assam tea, Coorg coffee, Gujarat cotton and Bengal jute — each crop has found its perfect home.
points: Cotton: a tropical kharif crop of semi-arid areas; India grows short staple (Indian) and long staple (American) cotton called 'narma' in the north-west; needs clear sky during flowering. Three areas: north-west (Punjab, Haryana, northern Rajasthan), west (Gujarat, Maharashtra) and south (plateaus of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu). Leading producers: Gujarat, Maharashtra and Telangana; India is among the world's top cotton producers.

Jute: used for coarse cloth, bags, sacks and decorative items; a cash crop of West Bengal and adjoining eastern parts; India lost large jute-growing areas to East Pakistan (Bangladesh) at partition. West Bengal produces about three-fourths of India's jute; Bihar and Assam are other jute areas.

Sugarcane: a tropical crop, rainfed in sub-humid and humid climates but largely irrigated in India; Uttar Pradesh produces about two-fifths; Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh are other leaders. India is the second largest producer after Brazil.

Tea: a plantation beverage crop introduced by the British in the 1840s in the Brahmaputra valley of Assam; later in Darjeeling, Jalpaiguri and Cooch Behar (West Bengal) and on lower slopes of the Nilgiri and Cardamom hills; grown on well-drained soils in humid and sub-humid tropics and subtropics. Assam produces more than half of India's tea; India is second after China.

Coffee: a tropical plantation crop with three varieties — arabica, robusta and liberica; India mostly grows superior arabica, in demand internationally; grown in the highlands of the Western Ghats in Karnataka, Kerala and Tamil Nadu; Karnataka produces more than two-thirds of India's coffee.

topics.title: Agricultural development and the Green Revolution

learn.hook: In the mid-1960s India imported foodgrains after two droughts. Within a decade, it became self-reliant. The Green Revolution changed everything.
points: Agriculture remains a very important sector: more than half of India's workforce (54.6% in Census 2011) depends on it for livelihood.

After Independence, the strategy was to increase foodgrain production by: switching from cash crops to food crops; intensification of cropping over already cultivated land; and bringing cultivable and fallow land under the plough.

In the 1960s, the Intensive Agricultural District Programme (IADP) and Intensive Agricultural Area Programme (IAAP) were launched; after two droughts in the mid-1960s caused a food crisis, high yielding varieties (HYVs) of wheat (from Mexico) and rice (from the Philippines) were introduced with chemical fertilisers in irrigated areas of Punjab, Haryana, western UP, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu — the Green Revolution. Assured irrigation was a basic prerequisite.

The Green Revolution made India self-reliant in foodgrains but was initially confined to irrigated areas, causing regional disparities until it spread to central and eastern India. In the 1980s the Planning Commission focused on rainfed areas; agro-climatic planning began in 1988, with diversification into dairy, poultry, horticulture, livestock and aquaculture. Liberalisation and the WTO in the 1990s exposed agriculture to international competition.

Output and yields of rice and wheat rose impressively; sugarcane, oilseeds and cotton also grew. As per NCERT data, India ranks first in pulses, jute, cattle and milk, and second in rice, wheat, groundnut, sugarcane and vegetables. Gross irrigated area and use of fertilisers and HYV seeds expanded greatly.

learn.hook: A large part of India's cropland still waits for the monsoon each year. One bad monsoon can push lakhs of farmers into debt.
points: Dependence on erratic monsoon: NCERT notes that irrigation covers only about one-third of the cultivated area (recent official data put it nearer half); the rest depends on rainfall, which is erratic — droughts and floods are common.

Low productivity: yields of most crops are low compared to international levels; high pressure on land and low labour productivity. Constraints of financial resources and indebtedness: inputs like HYVs, fertilisers and machinery are expensive; crop failures and low returns push farmers into debt and distress.

Lack of land reforms: unequal distribution of land and exploitation by landlords; land reforms were not effectively implemented. Small farm size and fragmentation: more than 60 per cent of ownership holdings are smaller than one hectare, and holdings are fragmented — uneconomic for modern farming.

Lack of commercialisation: many farmers grow crops for self-consumption; small farms cannot afford commercial crops. Vast underemployment: seasonal unemployment ranging from about 4 to 8 months in a year.

Degradation of cultivable land: faulty irrigation causes salinisation, alkalinisation and waterlogging; excessive chemicals reduce fertility; soil erosion by water and wind. Exam focus: fallow vs culturable wasteland, CPRs, dryland vs wetland, Green Revolution, problems and map marking.

topics.title: Water resources of India: the big numbers

learn.hook: India has about one-sixth of the world's people but only about 4% of its water. Every drop matters!
points: Water is a cyclic, renewable resource, but its quantity is limited; demand is rising while quality is declining.

India accounts for about 2.45 per cent of the world's surface area and 4 per cent of its water resources, but about one-sixth of its population (16 per cent in NCERT's figure; 17.5 per cent in Census 2011).
Total water available from precipitation in a year is about 4,000 cubic km; availability from surface water and replenishable groundwater is 1,869 cubic km.
Only about 60 per cent of this can be put to beneficial use, so the total utilisable water resource is only 1,122 cubic km.

learn.hook: The Ganga, Brahmaputra and Barak drain only about a third of India's area but carry about 60% of its surface water.
points: Surface water has four main sources: rivers, lakes, ponds and tanks.
India has about 10,360 rivers and tributaries longer than 1.6 km each; the mean annual flow in all river basins is estimated at 1,869 cubic km.
Due to topographical, hydrological and other constraints, only about 690 cubic km of surface water can be utilised.

Water flow in a river depends on the size of its catchment (river basin) and the rainfall within it. The Ganga, Brahmaputra and Barak have extremely large catchments with high rainfall; though covering only about one-third of the country's area, they have about 60 per cent of its surface water resources.
Much of the annual flow of south Indian rivers like the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri has been harnessed, but this is yet to be done in the Ganga and Brahmaputra basins.

learn.hook: In parts of Punjab, the water table has dropped so low that farmers must bore hundreds of feet. Groundwater is running out!
points: India's total replenishable groundwater resources are about 432 cubic km.
The Ganga and Brahmaputra basins have about 46 per cent of the total replenishable groundwater.
Groundwater utilisation is relatively high in river basins of the north-west and parts of south India — very high in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Tamil Nadu.
States like Gujarat, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Tripura and Maharashtra use groundwater at a moderate rate, while Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Kerala use only a small proportion of their potential.
If the present trend continues, demand will exceed supply; over-exploitation lowers the water table and can harm development and cause social disruption — so sustainable use is essential.

learn.hook: Kerala's backwaters, Odisha's Chilika and Bengal's coastal lakes hold huge amounts of water — but it is salty!
points: India has a vast and, in some states, highly indented coastline, which has led to the formation of many lagoons and lakes.

The water in these water bodies is generally brackish, but it is used for fishing and for irrigating certain varieties of paddy crops and coconut.
India has traditionally been an agrarian economy; about two-thirds of its population has depended on agriculture, so water demand is dominated by farming.

topics.title: Demand for irrigation and its problems

learn.hook: Punjab irrigates over 85% of its net sown area — and now worries about arsenic, fluoride and a vanishing water table.
points: Irrigation is needed because rainfall is unevenly distributed in space and time: large tracts (north-western India, Deccan plateau) are rainfall-deficient and drought-prone; winter and summer are dry in most parts; even in high-rainfall states like West Bengal and Bihar, breaks or failure of monsoon cause dry spells.
Some crops like rice, sugarcane and jute need a lot of water; multiple cropping is possible only with irrigation; HYV crops need regulated moisture.

Irrigation raises productivity: in Punjab, Haryana and western UP, more than 85 per cent of net sown area is irrigated, and wheat and rice there are grown mainly with irrigation, largely from wells and tube wells.

Problems of excessive irrigation: over-drawing of groundwater lowers the water table; fluoride concentration has increased in Rajasthan and Maharashtra and arsenic in West Bengal and Bihar; intensive irrigation also raises soil salinity.

topics.title: Emerging water problems: availability and pollution

learn.hook: The same Yamuna that is clear near its source becomes one of India's most polluted rivers after Delhi. What goes wrong?
points: Per capita availability of water is declining due to the increase in population.
Available water resources are also getting polluted by industrial, agricultural and domestic effluents, which limits usable water further.
Water quality refers to the purity of water, i.e. water without unwanted foreign substances; pollution happens when toxic substances enter lakes, streams, rivers, oceans and other water bodies.

Polluted water harms aquatic life and human health. CPCB data show organic and bacterial contamination as the main pollution source in rivers; the Yamuna is most polluted between Delhi and Etawah, and the Ganga is highly polluted at Kanpur and Varanasi; other polluted rivers include the Sabarmati at Ahmedabad, Gomti at Lucknow and Musi at Hyderabad.

example.q: If a city's water supply stays at 300 crore litres a day while its population rises from 1.5 crore to 2 crore, what happens to per capita supply?

topics.title: Water conservation: pollution control and recycling

learn.hook: A Bengaluru apartment treats its own sewage and uses it to flush toilets and water gardens — saving lakhs of litres of fresh water.
points: Declining availability and rising demand make conservation and effective management of water essential.

Strategies: water-saving technologies and methods, prevention of pollution, watershed development, rainwater harvesting, water recycling and reuse, conjunctive use of surface and groundwater, and long-term planning.

Prevention of pollution: the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), with State Pollution Control Boards, monitors water quality. Laws like the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 have not been implemented effectively; public awareness is needed.

Recycle and reuse: lower-quality reclaimed waste water can be used by industries for cooling and fire-fighting; in cities, water from bathing and washing utensils (and vehicle washing) can be used for gardening — reducing demand for fresh water.

example.q: Suggest two ways a factory and two ways a household can recycle water.
steps: Factory: use treated waste water for cooling; use it for fire-fighting.
Household: use bathing/utensil water for gardening; reuse vehicle-washing water for plants.
example.answer: Factory — cooling, fire-fighting; household — gardening with used water

learn.hook: Ralegan Siddhi, a drought-hit village in Maharashtra, turned green by building check dams and planting trees — through people's own efforts.
points: Watershed management means efficient management and conservation of surface and groundwater resources: preventing runoff, and storing and recharging groundwater through percolation tanks, recharge wells etc.
In a broad sense it includes conservation, regeneration and judicious use of all natural (land, water, plants, animals) and human resources within a watershed; community participation is essential.

Haryali: a Central Government–sponsored watershed project enabling rural people to conserve water for drinking, irrigation, fisheries and afforestation; executed by Gram Panchayats with people's participation.

Neeru-Meeru ('Water and You') in Andhra Pradesh and Arvary Pani Sansad in Alwar (Rajasthan) built water-harvesting structures like percolation tanks, dug-out ponds (johads) and check dams through people's participation.
Ralegan Siddhi (Ahmednagar district, Maharashtra) is a celebrated example of village-led watershed development that ended water scarcity.

learn.hook: Tamil Nadu made rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory for buildings — and Chennai's groundwater levels improved in response!
points: Rainwater harvesting is a method of capturing and storing rainwater for various uses; it is also used to recharge groundwater aquifers.
It is a low-cost and eco-friendly technique for preserving every drop of water by guiding rainwater to bore wells, pits and wells.
Traditional methods: lakes, ponds and irrigation tanks in rural areas; in Rajasthan, rainwater is stored in kunds or tankas (covered underground tanks) near houses or villages.

Benefits: increases water availability, checks the declining groundwater table, improves groundwater quality by diluting contaminants like fluoride and nitrates, prevents soil erosion and flooding, and arrests salt-water intrusion in coastal areas if used to recharge aquifers.
Tamil Nadu has made rooftop rainwater harvesting structures compulsory in all houses — no building can be constructed without them.

topics.title: National Water Policy and Jal Kranti Abhiyan

learn.hook: When water is scarce, who gets it first — farms, factories or families? India's National Water Policy answers: drinking water comes first.
points: The National Water Policy (2002) stipulates water allocation priorities: drinking water gets the top priority, followed by irrigation, hydropower and other uses such as industry and navigation.

Other NWP features: irrigation and multipurpose projects should include a drinking-water component; groundwater exploitation should be regulated; water quality should be improved; water should be conserved by efficient use; farmers and stakeholders should participate in management.

Jal Kranti Abhiyan (2015–16): aims to ensure water security through per capita availability of water; water-scarce villages in each district are selected as 'Jal Grams' for integrated water security plans; model command areas are developed; it promotes traditional and modern conservation with people's participation.
Exam focus: water figures (4,000; 1,869; 1,122; 432 cubic km), sectoral use, causes of declining water resources, emerging problems, watershed management and rainwater harvesting.

learn.hook: The iron in your bicycle, the copper in your phone charger and the mica in your iron box all came out of India's ancient rocks.
points: India is fortunate to have fairly rich and varied mineral resources due to its varied geological structure; most valuable minerals are products of pre-Palaeozoic age, associated with the metamorphic and igneous rocks of Peninsular India.
A mineral is a natural substance of organic or inorganic origin with definite chemical and physical properties.

Characteristics: minerals are unevenly distributed over space; there is an inverse relationship between quality and quantity — good quality minerals are less in quantity than low quality ones; all minerals are exhaustible, take long to develop geologically and cannot be replenished immediately.
Minerals are the base of industrial development — iron for steel, bauxite for aluminium, coal and oil for energy.

example.q: Why must minerals be used carefully even though India has many of them?
steps: Minerals are exhaustible.

example.answer: They are exhaustible and slow to form, and good quality deposits are few

learn.hook: Iron and copper are both metals — but one is 'ferrous' and the other isn't. And coal is a mineral too!
points: Minerals are of two main types: metallic and non-metallic.
Metallic minerals are sources of metals: ferrous minerals contain iron (iron ore, manganese, chromite); non-ferrous minerals do not contain iron (copper, bauxite, lead, zinc, gold).
Non-metallic minerals are either organic in origin — fossil fuels like coal and petroleum — or inorganic — mica, limestone, graphite.
Flowchart: Minerals → Metallic (Ferrous | Non-ferrous) and Non-metallic (Organic | Inorganic).

example.answer: Ferrous: chromite, manganese; non-ferrous: bauxite; organic: coal; inorganic: mica

topics.title: Distribution of minerals and the North-eastern Plateau belt

learn.hook: Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh sit on top of India's richest treasure chest of iron, coal and manganese.
points: Most metallic minerals in India occur in the old crystalline rocks of the Peninsular plateau.
Over 97 per cent of coal reserves occur in the valleys of the Damodar, Sone, Mahanadi and Godavari.
Petroleum reserves are in the sedimentary basins of Assam, Gujarat and Mumbai High (offshore in the Arabian Sea); new reserves have been found in the Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri basins.
Minerals are concentrated in three broad belts, plus scattered occurrences: the North-eastern Plateau region, the South-western Plateau region and the North-western region.
North-eastern Plateau region: covers Chotanagpur (Jharkhand), the Odisha plateau, West Bengal and parts of Chhattisgarh; has a variety of minerals — iron ore, coal, manganese, bauxite and mica.

topics.title: South-western, North-western and Himalayan mineral belts

learn.hook: Rajasthan's marble built the Taj Mahal; Karnataka's Kolar gave India its gold; Kerala's beaches hide thorium-rich monazite.
points: South-western Plateau region: Karnataka, Goa and contiguous Tamil Nadu uplands and Kerala; rich in ferrous metals and bauxite; high-grade iron ore, manganese and limestone; Neyveli lignite (Tamil Nadu); monazite sands in Kerala; Kolar gold mines (Karnataka). It is less diversified than the North-eastern belt.

North-western region: along the Aravalis in Rajasthan and part of Gujarat; non-ferrous minerals like copper and zinc; building stones — sandstone, granite, marble; gypsum and Fuller's earth; dolomite and limestone for cement; Gujarat has petroleum; salt from Gujarat and Rajasthan.
Himalayan belt: copper, lead, zinc, cobalt and tungsten occur in the east and west; Assam valley has mineral oil deposits; oil is also found offshore near Mumbai (Mumbai High).
Map reading: shade the three belts — NE plateau (Jharkhand–Odisha–Chhattisgarh), SW plateau (Karnataka–Goa–Kerala) and NW (Rajasthan–Gujarat).

learn.hook: No steel without manganese, no aluminium without bauxite. Odisha leads India in both!
points: Manganese is an important raw material for smelting iron ore and for making ferro alloys; its deposits occur in almost all geological formations but mainly in the Dharwar system.

Odisha is the leading manganese producer (Bonai, Kendujhar, Sundergarh, Gangpur, Koraput, Kalahandi, Bolangir); Karnataka (Dharwar, Ballari, Belagavi, North Canara, Chikkamagaluru, Shivamogga, Chitradurga, Tumakuru); Maharashtra (Nagpur, Bhandara, Ratnagiri — far from steel plants); Madhya Pradesh (Balaghat–Chhindwara–Nimar–Mandla–Jhabua belt); Telangana, Goa and Jharkhand are minor producers.
India is poorly endowed with non-ferrous metallic minerals except bauxite.
Bauxite is the ore used to make aluminium; it is found mainly in tertiary deposits associated with laterite rocks on the plateaus or hill ranges of Peninsular India and in coastal tracts.

Odisha is the largest bauxite producer (Kalahandi and Sambalpur leading; Bolangir, Koraput); the patlands of Lohardaga (Jharkhand); Gujarat (Bhavnagar, Jamnagar); Chhattisgarh (Amarkantak plateau); Madhya Pradesh (Katni–Jabalpur, Balaghat); Maharashtra (Kolaba, Thane, Ratnagiri, Satara, Pune, Kolhapur).

topics.title: Copper, mica and other non-metallic minerals

learn.hook: The copper in your house wiring may come from Khetri in Rajasthan, and the mica in old electrical insulation from the Gaya–Hazaribagh belt.
points: Copper is indispensable in the electrical industry for wires, electric motors, transformers and generators; it is alloyable, malleable and ductile, and is mixed with gold to give strength to jewellery.

Copper deposits mainly occur in Singhbhum district (Jharkhand), Balaghat district (Madhya Pradesh) and Jhunjhunu (Khetri) and Alwar districts (Rajasthan); minor producers: Agnigundala (Guntur, Andhra Pradesh), Chitradurga and Hassan (Karnataka), South Arcot (Tamil Nadu).
Mica is used mainly in electrical and electronic industries; it can be split into very thin sheets that are tough and flexible.

Mica areas: in Jharkhand, high-quality mica comes from a belt about 150 km long and 32 km wide from Gaya to Hazaribagh; Nellore (Andhra Pradesh) produces the best quality mica; in Rajasthan, a belt of about 320 km from Jaipur to Bhilwara and around Udaipur (with Ajmer and Beawar); also Karnataka (Mysuru, Hassan), Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and West Bengal.

Other non-metallic minerals include limestone, dolomite and phosphate (used in cement, steel flux and fertilisers). Map work: copper — Hazaribagh, Singhbhum, Khetri; bauxite — Katni, Bilaspur, Koraput; mica — Ajmer, Beawar, Nellore, Gaya, Hazaribagh.

topics.title: Coal: uses, types and Damodar valley fields

learn.hook: Most of India's electricity is still generated by burning coal — much of it dug from Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh.
points: Mineral fuels are essential for generating power, needed by agriculture, industry, transport and other sectors.
Coal is mainly used in thermal power generation and in smelting of iron ore.

Coal in India occurs in rock sequences of two main geological ages: Gondwana (a little over 200 million years old), which holds most of the reserves, and Tertiary (about 55 million years old). About 80 per cent of Indian coal is bituminous and of non-coking grade.
The most important Gondwana coalfields are in the Damodar valley, in the Jharkhand–Bengal coal belt: Raniganj, Jharia, Bokaro, Giridih and Karanpura.
Jharia is the largest coalfield, followed by Raniganj.

learn.hook: Coal under Cherrapunji, the rainiest place on Earth? Yes — the north-east has young Tertiary coal.

Tertiary coals occur in Assam, Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya and Nagaland: Darangiri, Cherrapunji, Mewlong and Langrin (Meghalaya); Makum, Jaipur and Nazira (upper Assam); Namchik–Namphuk (Arunachal Pradesh); and Kalakot (Jammu and Kashmir).

learn.hook: Mumbai High, 160 km out in the Arabian Sea, was discovered in 1973 and changed India's oil story.
points: Crude petroleum consists of hydrocarbons in liquid and gaseous states, varying in chemical composition, colour and specific gravity; it occurs in sedimentary rocks of the Tertiary period.

It is essential for internal combustion engines in automobiles, railways and aircraft; its by-products feed petrochemical industries — fertilisers, synthetic rubber, synthetic fibre, medicines, vaseline, lubricants, wax, soap and cosmetics. Its value and many uses earn it the name 'liquid gold'.
Oil exploration became systematic after the Oil and Natural Gas Commission (ONGC) was set up in 1956; until then Digboi in Assam (where oil was struck in 1889) was the only oil-producing region.

Oil fields: Assam — Digboi, Naharkatiya, Moran; Gujarat — Ankaleshwar, Kalol, Mehsana, Nawagam, Kosamba, Lunej; Mumbai High (offshore, discovered 1973, production from 1976); Krishna–Godavari and Kaveri basins. Refineries are field-based (e.g. Digboi) or market-based (e.g. Barauni); map work: Mathura, Jamnagar, Barauni refineries.

Natural gas: the Gas Authority of India Limited (GAIL) was set up in 1984 to transport and market natural gas; it is found with oil in all fields, with exclusive reserves along the east coast (Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh), Tripura, Rajasthan and offshore wells of Gujarat and Maharashtra.

steps: Digboi is located on an oil field → field-based.
Barauni is located near consumers, away from oil fields → market-based.
example.answer: Digboi — field-based; Barauni — market-based

learn.hook: Kerala's black beach sands hold some of the world's richest thorium deposits — fuel for India's future nuclear plans.
points: Uranium and thorium are the important minerals used to generate nuclear energy.

Uranium deposits occur in Dharwar rocks: along the Singhbhum copper belt (Jaduguda, Jharkhand); Udaipur, Alwar and Jhunjhunu (Rajasthan); Durg (Chhattisgarh); Bhandara (Maharashtra); and Kullu (Himachal Pradesh).

Thorium is obtained mainly from monazite and ilmenite in beach sands along the coasts of Kerala and Tamil Nadu; the world's richest monazite deposits occur in Palakkad and Kollam districts of Kerala, near Visakhapatnam (Andhra Pradesh) and in the Mahanadi delta (Odisha).
The Atomic Energy Commission was set up in 1948; real progress came after the Atomic Energy Institute at Trombay was set up in 1954, renamed the Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) in 1967.
Nuclear power projects: Tarapur (Maharashtra), Rawatbhata near Kota (Rajasthan), Kalpakkam (Tamil Nadu), Narora (Uttar Pradesh), Kaiga (Karnataka) and Kakrapar (Gujarat).

learn.hook: Rajasthan's Bhadla solar park, one of the world's largest, sits where the sun shines almost every day of the year.
points: Fossil fuels are exhaustible and cause pollution; non-conventional sources — solar, wind, hydro-geothermal and biomass — are renewable, more equitably distributed and environment-friendly.

Solar energy is tapped by photovoltaic cells and solar thermal technology; solar thermal is cost-competitive, environment-friendly and easy to construct; used in heaters, crop dryers and cookers. Western India (Gujarat, Rajasthan) has great potential.

Wind energy is absolutely pollution-free and inexhaustible; turbines convert the kinetic energy of wind into electricity; permanent winds, monsoon winds, local winds and land and sea breezes can be used. Rajasthan, Gujarat, Maharashtra and Karnataka have favourable conditions.

Tidal and wave energy: ocean currents are a store-house of infinite energy; large tidal waves occur along the west coast (e.g. Gulf of Kachchh and Gulf of Khambhat), so India has great potential, not yet utilised. Geothermal energy: heat from the earth's interior, tapped via hot springs and geysers; a plant has been commissioned at Manikaran (Himachal Pradesh); Puga valley (Ladakh) also has potential.

Bio-energy: energy from biological products — agricultural residues, municipal, industrial and other wastes; it can give electricity, heat or cooking gas, improve the rural economy, reduce pollution and pressure on fuel wood. Example: the waste-to-energy project at Okhla, Delhi.

example.q: Suggest the best non-conventional source for: (a) Jaisalmer; (b) Gulf of Khambhat; (c) Manikaran; (d) a village with lots of cattle dung.
steps: (a) Sunny desert → solar.
(b) High tides → tidal energy.
(c) Hot springs → geothermal.
(d) Cattle dung and farm waste → bio-energy (biogas).
example.answer: (a) solar, (b) tidal, (c) geothermal, (d) bio-energy

topics.title: Conservation of mineral and energy resources

learn.hook: An old aluminium can melted and remade uses about 95% less energy than making new aluminium from bauxite. Recycling is mining above ground!
points: Sustainable development requires integrating economic development with environmental concerns, conserving minerals and energy for future generations.
Alternative energy sources like solar, wind, wave and geothermal energy are inexhaustible and should be developed to replace exhaustible sources.

For metallic minerals, using scrap metals enables recycling — especially important for copper, lead and zinc, of which India's reserves are meagre. Using substitutes for scarce metals can also reduce consumption.
Export of strategic and scarce minerals must be reduced so that existing reserves last longer; improved mining techniques can reduce wastage.

Exam focus: classification of minerals; distribution of iron ore, manganese, bauxite, coal and petroleum; nuclear minerals; non-conventional energy; conservation measures; and map marking of mines and refineries.

chapters.title: India: Planning and Sustainable Development in Indian Context

topics.title: Planning: meaning, sectoral and regional planning

learn.hook: From 1951 to 2017, India ran its economy through Five Year Plans. Why plan at all — and plan for whom: sectors or regions?
points: Planning is the process of thinking, formulating a scheme or programme and implementing a set of actions to achieve some goal.
In India, planning was done through Five Year Plans prepared by the Planning Commission, set up in 1950; the First Five Year Plan began in 1951.

Sectoral planning: formulating and implementing schemes for development of various sectors of the economy — agriculture, irrigation, manufacturing, power, construction, transport, communication, social infrastructure and services.
Regional planning: development is not uniform over space; some regions are more developed than others, so regional planning aims to reduce regional imbalances in development.

steps: The plan targets a particular region (backward districts).
Its aim is to reduce imbalance with other regions.
So it is regional planning.
example.answer: Regional planning

topics.title: NITI Aayog and target area planning

learn.hook: On 1 January 2015, the 65-year-old Planning Commission was replaced by a 'think tank' — NITI Aayog.
points: NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015. It acts as a think tank giving strategic and technical advice to the Central and State Governments, follows a bottom-up, decentralised approach and promotes cooperative federalism.
To arrest growing regional and social disparities, the Planning Commission introduced target area and target group approaches.
Target area programmes: Command Area Development Programme, Drought Prone Area Programme, Desert Development Programme and Hill Area Development Programme.
Target group programmes: Small Farmers Development Agency (SFDA) and Marginal Farmers Development Agency (MFDA).
In the Eighth Five Year Plan, special area programmes were designed to develop infrastructure in hill areas, north-eastern states, tribal areas and backward areas.

learn.hook: Apple orchards in Uttarakhand, tea in Darjeeling, Nilgiri dairy cooperatives — hill development must suit the hills.
points: The Hill Area Development Programme was initiated during the Fifth Five Year Plan, covering 15 districts: all the hilly districts of Uttar Pradesh (now Uttarakhand), Mikir Hill and North Cachar hills of Assam, Darjeeling district of West Bengal and Nilgiri district of Tamil Nadu.

The National Committee on the Development of Backward Areas (1981) recommended that all hill areas with a height above 600 m and not covered under the tribal sub-plan be treated as backward hill areas.
Detailed plans were drawn to harness indigenous resources through horticulture, plantation agriculture, animal husbandry, poultry, forestry, and small-scale and village industries.
The plans were to take into account the topography, ecological, social and economic conditions of each area.

topics.title: Drought Prone Area Programme: aims and approach

learn.hook: In a drought year, a farmer in Marathwada loses his crop and his income. DPAP tried to give him work — and long-term water security.
points: The Drought Prone Area Programme (DPAP) was initiated during the Fourth Five Year Plan with the objectives of providing employment to people in drought-prone areas and creating productive assets.
Initially it emphasised the construction of labour-intensive civil works.

Later it emphasised irrigation projects, land development programmes, afforestation, grassland development and creation of basic rural infrastructure such as electricity, roads, markets, credit and services.
The National Committee on Development of Backward Areas found that the programme was largely confined to agriculture and allied sectors, with a major focus on restoration of ecological balance.

example.q: Why did DPAP shift from labour-intensive civil works to irrigation, afforestation and grassland development?
steps: Civil works gave short-term jobs but not lasting drought-proofing.
Irrigation, afforestation and pastures build productive assets and restore ecology.
These reduce the impact of future droughts.
example.answer: To create lasting productive assets and restore ecological balance

topics.title: Drought-prone areas of India and watershed approach

learn.hook: Rajasthan, Marathwada, Rayalaseema, Telangana — these names often appear in drought headlines. Why these regions?
points: Growing population pressure forces people to use marginal lands for agriculture, causing ecological degradation; so alternative employment opportunities are needed in drought-prone areas.
The strategy for these areas is an integrated watershed development approach at the micro level: restoring ecological balance among water, soil, plants, and human and animal populations.

In 1967 the Planning Commission identified 67 districts (entirely or partly) as drought-prone; in 1972 the Irrigation Commission introduced the criterion of 30 per cent irrigated area to demarcate drought-prone areas.

Drought-prone areas mostly cover the semi-arid and arid tracts of Rajasthan, Gujarat, western Madhya Pradesh, Marathwada (Maharashtra), the Rayalaseema and Telangana plateaus, the Karnataka plateau and the highlands and interior parts of Tamil Nadu.
Drought-prone areas of Punjab, Haryana and northern Rajasthan are largely protected because of the spread of irrigation.

learn.hook: High in the Himachal Himalayas, the Gaddi shepherds of Bharmaur move their flocks with the seasons, speaking their own Gaddiali dialect.
points: The Bharmaur tribal area comprises the Bharmaur and Holi tehsils of Chamba district, Himachal Pradesh; it has been a notified tribal area since 21 November 1975.
It is inhabited by the Gaddis, a tribal community who have maintained a distinct identity in the Himalayan region; they practised transhumance and converse in the Gaddiali dialect.

The region has harsh climatic conditions, a low resource base and a fragile environment. The Ravi and its tributaries, the Budhil and Tundahen, drain it and carve deep gorges; it lies between the Dhaula Dhar range (south) and Pir Panjal (north) and has four physiographic divisions — Holi, Khani, Kugti and Tundah.
Winters are freezing with snowfall (mean January temperature about 4°C); summers are mild (July about 26°C). Gaddis traditionally migrate to lower areas in winter.

The economy was based on agriculture and allied activities like sheep and goat rearing; the region was economically and socially backward and isolated. On a map, Bharmaur lies in Chamba district in the north-west of Himachal Pradesh.

topics.title: Bharmaur: Integrated Tribal Development Project and outcomes

learn.hook: In 1971, fewer than 2 in 100 women in Bharmaur could read. By 2011, about 65 did. What changed?
points: Development of Bharmaur began in the 1970s when the Gaddis were included among Scheduled Tribes. The tribal sub-plan was introduced in 1974 under the Fifth Five Year Plan, and Bharmaur was designated as one of five Integrated Tribal Development Projects (ITDP) in Himachal Pradesh.

Aim: improve the quality of life of the Gaddis and narrow the gap in development between Bharmaur and other areas of Himachal Pradesh; highest priority to transport and communications, agriculture and allied activities, and social and community services.

Outcomes: infrastructure — schools, health care facilities, potable water, roads, communications and electricity. Villages along the Ravi in Holi and Khani areas benefited most; remote villages in Tundah and Kugti are still outside the ambit of development.

Social benefits: big rise in literacy, improved sex ratio and decline in child marriage; female literacy rose from 1.88 per cent in 1971 to 65 per cent in 2011, and the gender gap in literacy declined.

Economic change: shift from subsistence agro-pastoral economy (foodgrains, livestock) to more pulses and cash crops (though with traditional tools); only about one-tenth of households now practise transhumance, and many Gaddis migrate to Kangra and nearby areas in winter for wage labour.

example.q: By how many percentage points did female literacy in Bharmaur rise from 1971 to 2011?
steps: Increase = 65 − 1.88 = 63.12 percentage points.
example.answer: 63.12 percentage points

learn.reallife: Roads and schools under ITDP connected Holi and Khani villages to Chamba town, opening jobs and colleges to young Gaddis.

learn.hook: In 1987, a commission led by Norway's Prime Minister gave the world a definition of development that every exam still asks for.
points: The concept of development has changed: earlier it meant economic growth (GNP, per capita income); later it came to include social welfare and qualitative change in people's lives.
In the late 1960s, growing environmental awareness in the western world was reflected in books like 'The Population Bomb' by Ehrlich (1968) and 'The Limits to Growth' by Meadows and others (1972).

The United Nations set up the World Commission on Environment and Development (WCED), headed by Norwegian Prime Minister Gro Harlem Brundtland; its report 'Our Common Future' (1987), also called the Brundtland Report, popularised sustainable development.
Sustainable development: development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs.
It integrates ecological, social and economic aspects of development; the UN's 17 Sustainable Development Goals (adopted in 2015) carry this idea forward.

example.q: A town wants to grow by cutting down its watershed forest for housing. Using the Brundtland definition, explain why this may not be sustainable.
steps: It meets present housing needs.
But it destroys the forest that protects water and soil for the future.
This compromises future generations' ability to meet their needs.
example.answer: It meets present needs at the cost of future generations

topics.title: Indira Gandhi Canal: origin, stages and command area

learn.hook: A canal running hundreds of kilometres through the Thar desert, parallel to the Pakistan border — the Indira Gandhi Canal turned sand into fields.
points: The Indira Gandhi Canal (earlier the Rajasthan Canal) is one of the largest canal systems in India; conceived by Kanwar Sain in 1948, it was launched on 31 March 1958.
It originates at the Harike barrage in Punjab and runs parallel to the Pakistan border at an average distance of 40 km in the Thar desert (Marusthali) of Rajasthan.
The total planned length of the system is 9,060 km, serving a culturable command area of 19.63 lakh hectares; about 70 per cent was to be irrigated by flow and the rest by lift irrigation.

Stage I: command area in Ganganagar, Hanumangarh and northern Bikaner districts; gently undulating topography; culturable command area 5.53 lakh ha; irrigation from the early 1960s. Stage II: Bikaner, Jaisalmer, Barmer, Jodhpur, Nagaur and Churu districts; desert with shifting sand dunes and summer temperatures up to 50°C; command area 14.10 lakh ha; irrigation from the mid-1980s.
In lift canals, water is lifted up to make it flow against the slope of the land. Map reading: trace the canal from Harike (Punjab) south-west through Ganganagar to Jaisalmer and Barmer.

example.answer: 19.63 lakh hectares

topics.title: Indira Gandhi Canal: positive and negative impacts

learn.hook: Where camels once grazed on bajra stubble, farmers now grow wheat and cotton — but some fields have turned white with salt.
points: Positive impacts: availability of soil moisture increased; afforestation and pasture development programmes greened the land; soil erosion, wind erosion and siltation of canals reduced; canal water also met drinking water needs.
Agricultural changes: cultivated area and intensity of cropping increased tremendously.
Traditional crops — gram, bajra and guar — have been replaced by wheat, cotton, groundnut and rice.
Negative impacts: intensive irrigation and excessive use of water have led to the twin environmental problems of waterlogging and soil salinity, raising doubts about long-term sustainability.

example.q: Why does excessive canal irrigation in a desert cause soil salinity?
steps: Too much water raises the water table (waterlogging).
In high heat, water evaporates from the surface.
Dissolved salts are left behind on the soil — salinity.
example.answer: Waterlogging plus high evaporation leaves salts on the surface

learn.reallife: Parts of the canal command area now need drainage and gypsum treatment to reclaim salt-affected soils.

topics.title: Sustainable development in the canal area: water and land measures

learn.hook: Warabandi: a rotating timetable that gives every farmer on a canal outlet a fair turn of water. Simple idea, big impact!
points: The first and foremost requirement is strict implementation of the water management policy: protective irrigation in Stage I, and extensive irrigation of crops and pasture development in Stage II.
The cropping pattern should not include water-intensive crops; people should be encouraged to grow plantation crops such as citrus fruits instead.

Command Area Development (CAD) programmes — lining of watercourses, land development and levelling, and the warabandi system (equal distribution of canal water in the command area of an outlet) — should be implemented to reduce conveyance loss of water.
Areas affected by waterlogging and soil salinity should be reclaimed.

example.q: Why is lining of watercourses an important CAD measure?
steps: Unlined channels lose water by seepage into sandy soil.
Seepage raises the water table and causes waterlogging.
Lining reduces conveyance loss and waterlogging.
example.answer: It cuts seepage losses and reduces waterlogging

learn.reallife: Kinnow and other citrus orchards around Ganganagar show how less water-intensive plantation crops can thrive with canal water.

topics.title: Transport and communication: lifelines of the economy

learn.hook: Every packet of Amul butter in Guwahati, every Aadhaar SMS in a village — all depend on India's transport and communication networks.
points: Transport and communication are the lifelines of an economy: they move goods, services, people and ideas from places of production to places of consumption.
Their means evolved from ancient routes — the Grand Trunk road and the Silk Route — to modern road, rail, air and digital networks.
Modes of transport: land (roads and railways), water (inland waterways and oceanic routes), air and pipelines.
Communication may be personal (letters, phone, internet) or mass communication (radio, television, newspapers, films).

example.q: Classify: (a) a WhatsApp message to a friend; (b) a Doordarshan news bulletin; (c) a goods train; (d) an oil pipeline.

learn.hook: Sher Shah Suri's Shahi road ran from Sonargaon in Bengal to Peshawar. Today its stretch from Amritsar to Kolkata is still busy!
points: Pathways and unmetalled roads have been used since ancient times; modern roads developed with economic and technological growth.

Sher Shah Suri built the Shahi (Royal) road from Sonargaon (now in Bangladesh) to Peshawar (now in Pakistan); the British renamed it the Grand Trunk (GT) road, connecting Calcutta (Kolkata) and Peshawar. Today it extends from Amritsar to Kolkata.
India has one of the largest road networks in the world, over 60 lakh km long; about 85 per cent of passenger and 70 per cent of freight traffic are carried by road every year.
Road development plans: the Nagpur Plan (1943) and the twenty-year road plan (1961).

topics.title: Classification of roads and National Highways

learn.hook: National Highways are only about 2% of India's road length — yet they carry about 40% of road traffic!
points: For construction and maintenance, roads are classified as National Highways, State Highways, District Roads, Rural Roads and other roads (Border Roads and International Highways).

National Highways (NH) are constructed and maintained by the Central Government; they are used for inter-state transport and movement of defence personnel and material in strategic areas; they connect state capitals, major cities, ports and railway junctions.
NHs constitute only about 2 per cent of total road length but carry about 40 per cent of road traffic.
The National Highways Authority of India (NHAI), operationalised in 1995, is an autonomous body under the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways that develops, maintains and operates NHs.
Major NHAI projects: the Golden Quadrilateral (Delhi–Mumbai–Chennai–Kolkata), the North–South Corridor (Srinagar to Kanyakumari) and the East–West Corridor (Silchar in Assam to Porbandar in Gujarat).

example.q: Name the end points of the North–South and East–West corridors and where they cross India's four metros route.
steps: North–South: Srinagar (J&K) to Kanyakumari (Tamil Nadu).
East–West: Silchar (Assam) to Porbandar (Gujarat).
Both intersect the Golden Quadrilateral linking Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata.
example.answer: NS: Srinagar–Kanyakumari; EW: Silchar–Porbandar

topics.title: State highways, district and rural roads, border roads and road density

learn.hook: The Manali–Leh road climbs over passes above 5,000 m and stays open only a few months a year. Who builds roads like that?
points: State Highways are constructed and maintained by state governments; they join state capitals with district headquarters and other important towns.
District roads connect district headquarters with other important nodes in the district; they are maintained by the Zila Parishad.

Rural roads are vital for providing links in rural areas; about 80 per cent of total road length is rural roads. The Pradhan Mantri Grameen Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) aims to link every village to a major town by an all-season motorable road.

Other roads: Border roads — the Border Roads Organisation (BRO), established in May 1960, builds strategically important roads along northern and north-eastern borders, e.g. Chandigarh–Manali–Leh road (average altitude about 4,270 m). International highways promote harmonious relationships with neighbouring countries.
Road distribution is uneven: road density is highest in Kerala and lowest in Jammu and Kashmir (and Ladakh) — affected by terrain and level of economic development.

example.q: Why is road density low in Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh but high in Kerala?
steps: J&K and Ladakh: mountainous, rugged terrain, snow, sparse population → costly to build roads.
Kerala: plains and coastal lowlands, dense population, high development.
So density differs with terrain and economy.
example.answer: Rugged terrain and sparse population vs plains, dense population and development

topics.title: Indian Railways: history, network and gauges

learn.hook: On 16 April 1853, India's first train puffed 34 km from Bombay to Thane. Today Indian Railways carries crores of passengers every day.
points: Indian Railways is a major mode for long-distance freight and passenger traffic; the first train ran from Mumbai to Thane in 1853, covering 34 km.
It is one of the largest government undertakings in India, with a network of about 68,000 route km, divided into zones for administration.
Gauges: broad gauge (1.676 m), metre gauge (1 m) and narrow gauges (0.762 m and 0.610 m). Under Project Unigauge, metre and narrow gauge lines are being converted to broad gauge.
Metro rail: Kolkata got India's first metro in 1984; Delhi and many other cities followed. Steam engines have been replaced by diesel and electric locomotives.

topics.title: Konkan Railway and railways for tourism and freight

learn.hook: The Konkan Railway crosses 146 rivers and runs through 73 tunnels along the Western Ghats. Engineers call it a marvel!
points: The Konkan Railway, completed in 1998, is a 760 km route connecting Roha in Maharashtra to Mangaluru in Karnataka.
It is an engineering marvel: it crosses 146 rivers and streams, nearly 2,000 bridges and 73 tunnels; its longest tunnel, nearly 6.5 km long, was described by NCERT as Asia's largest.
Maharashtra, Goa and Karnataka are partners in this undertaking.
Railways also promote tourism — the Palace on Wheels, and heritage mountain railways like the Darjeeling Himalayan Railway and Nilgiri Mountain Railway (UNESCO World Heritage).
Dedicated Freight Corridors (Eastern and Western) are being built so that goods trains can run faster on separate tracks, freeing passenger lines.

Oceanic routes: India has a coastline of about 7,517 km including islands; 12 major and about 200 minor ports provide infrastructure.
About 95 per cent of India's foreign trade by volume and 70 per cent by value moves through oceanic routes; they are also used for coastal transport within the country.

learn.hook: India's air story began in 1911 with an airmail flight of just 10 km — from Allahabad across the river to Naini!
points: Air transport is the fastest, most comfortable and prestigious mode; it can cover very difficult terrain like high mountains, dreary deserts, dense forests and long oceanic stretches.

Air transport in India began in 1911, when airmail operated over 10 km between Allahabad and Naini. The Airports Authority of India provides safe and efficient air traffic and aeronautical communication services.

Air India provides international and domestic services; air transport was nationalised in 1953; Indian Airlines later merged with Air India, and Air India was privatised in 2022 (acquired by the Tata group).

Pawan Hans Helicopters Ltd provides helicopter services to ONGC's offshore operations and to inaccessible areas and difficult terrains like the north-eastern states and the interiors of J&K, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand; it also serves tourism.

UDAN (Ude Desh ka Aam Nagrik) is a regional connectivity scheme to make flying affordable and connect smaller towns. Map work: mark major international airports (Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata, Bengaluru, Hyderabad) and domestic airports.

example.answer: It overcomes difficult terrain and connects remote areas quickly

learn.hook: Asia's first cross-country oil pipeline ran 1,157 km from Naharkatiya in Assam to Barauni in Bihar.
points: Pipelines are the most convenient and efficient mode for transporting liquids and gases over long distances; even solids can be transported after converting them into slurry.

Oil India Limited (OIL), under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, is engaged in exploration, production and transportation of crude oil and natural gas; it built Asia's first cross-country pipeline (1,157 km) from Naharkatiya oilfield (Assam) to Barauni refinery (Bihar), later extended to Kanpur.
In western India, important pipelines include Ankaleshwar–Koyali, Mumbai High–Koyali and the Salaya–Koyali–Mathura pipeline from Gujarat to Mathura (with a branch towards Panipat and Jalandhar).

The Gas Authority of India Limited (GAIL), set up in 1984, built the Hazira–Vijaipur–Jagdishpur (HVJ) gas pipeline, linking Mumbai High and Bassein gas fields with fertiliser, power and industrial complexes in western and northern India.
Pipelines reduce the load on roads and railways, give continuous supply with low running cost and little transit loss; Indian Oil operates an extensive pipeline network.

example.q: Why was a pipeline from Naharkatiya to Barauni preferred over rail tankers?
steps: Oil had to travel over 1,100 km from Assam to Bihar.
Pipelines give continuous, low-cost flow with little loss.
They free railways for other traffic.
example.answer: Continuous, cheap, low-loss transport over a long distance

topics.title: Communication networks: personal and mass communication

learn.hook: India Post has over 1.5 lakh post offices — the largest postal network in the world — while India also has one of the world's largest mobile phone networks.
points: Communication has evolved from drum beats, messengers and pigeons to modern telecommunications; it can be personal or mass communication.

Personal communication: the postal service (the largest postal network in the world), telegraph, telephone, mobile phones and the internet. The internet (e-mail, e-commerce, e-governance) is used mostly in urban areas, and the Digital India initiative aims to spread it widely.
Telecommunication: India's mobile phone network is among the largest in the world; Subscriber Trunk Dialling (STD) and optical fibre cables enabled fast long-distance calls and data.

Mass communication: radio broadcasting began in 1923 (Radio Club of Bombay); the government named it All India Radio in 1936 and Akashvani in 1957. Television broadcasting began in 1959; Doordarshan is the national broadcaster with one of the largest terrestrial networks.

Press: newspapers are published in many languages, with Hindi newspapers being the largest in number. Films: India is the largest producer of feature films in the world; the Central Board of Film Certification certifies films.

learn.hook: Every weather forecast you see on TV uses images from India's own INSAT satellites — and crop and forest maps come from IRS satellites.
points: Satellites are a mode of communication in themselves and also regulate other means of communication; satellite images are used for weather forecasting, monitoring natural calamities, surveillance of border areas and more.
India's satellite system can be grouped into the Indian National Satellite System (INSAT) and the Indian Remote Sensing Satellite System (IRS).
INSAT, established in 1983, is a multi-purpose satellite system for telecommunications, meteorological observation and broadcasting.

The IRS system became operational with the launch of IRS-1A in March 1988; it gives data for resource monitoring and management. The National Remote Sensing Centre (NRSC) at Hyderabad acquires and processes data; ISRO runs India's space programme.
Exam focus: road classification and NH, BRO, Konkan Railway, national waterways, pipelines, satellite communication, mass communication, and road vs rail transport.

learn.hook: India sells medicines to Africa, rice to the Gulf and software to the USA, and buys crude oil, gold and electronics. No country is self-sufficient.
points: International trade is the exchange of goods and services among countries; no country is self-sufficient, so trade is necessary.
India's share in world trade is small (NCERT puts it at about 1 per cent), but India is an integral part of the world economy and its trade has grown rapidly.
Exports are goods and services sold abroad; imports are those bought from abroad.
Balance of trade = exports − imports; it is favourable (positive) if exports exceed imports and unfavourable (negative) if imports exceed exports.

topics.title: Changing pattern of India's trade and the trade deficit

learn.hook: In 1950–51 India's total trade was a little over ₹1,200 crore. Today it runs into lakhs of crores. What drove this boom?
points: The volume of India's international trade has increased manifold since 1950–51 (from about ₹1,214 crore then to many lakh crore today).
Reasons for growth: momentum in the manufacturing sector, liberal policies of the government (especially after liberalisation in 1991), and diversification of markets.
Imports have consistently exceeded exports, so India has a trade deficit (negative balance of trade) that has been increasing.
Reasons for the rising deficit include the price rise of crude petroleum in the international market, and large imports of gold, electronics and machinery.
Graphs of India's exports, imports and trade balance over the years show both lines rising, with imports above exports and the deficit widening.

example.q: In a year, India's exports are ₹25 lakh crore and imports ₹40 lakh crore. Next year exports are ₹30 lakh crore and imports ₹48 lakh crore. Did the deficit widen?
steps: Year 1 deficit = 25 − 40 = −15.
Year 2 deficit = 30 − 48 = −18.
Deficit widened by 3 lakh crore.
example.answer: Yes — from −15 to −18 lakh crore

learn.hook: In the 1960s, India imported wheat under the PL-480 scheme to avoid famine. After the Green Revolution, it stopped importing grain — and started importing oil and fertilisers.

Machinery and equipment, special steel, edible oil and chemicals largely make up the import basket.
Imports of petroleum and petroleum products have increased greatly — used both as fuel and as industrial raw material — reflecting rising industrialisation and a better standard of living.

topics.title: Sea ports as gateways of trade

learn.hook: When Karachi went to Pakistan in 1947, India lost its main western port overnight. So it built a brand-new one — Kandla.
points: India is surrounded by sea on three sides; ports are gateways of international trade, and about 95 per cent of India's trade by volume moves by sea.
India has a coastline of about 7,517 km with 12 major ports and about 200 minor or intermediate ports.
Major ports are under the control of the Central Government; minor ports are controlled by state governments.
Ports such as Kolkata, Mumbai and Chennai were developed by the British as suction points for India's resources and as entry points for their manufactured goods.
After partition, India lost Karachi port to Pakistan and Chittagong to East Pakistan; to compensate, Kandla was developed on the west coast and Diamond Harbour near Kolkata on the east.

example.q: Why was Kandla port developed after 1947?
steps: Karachi, the main port for north-western India, went to Pakistan.
Mumbai alone could not handle all western traffic.
So Kandla was built on the Gulf of Kachchh to ease the pressure.
example.answer: To replace Karachi and ease pressure on Mumbai

topics.title: West coast ports I: Kandla, Mumbai and JNPT

learn.hook: Nhava Sheva (JNPT), across the harbour from Mumbai, handles the largest share of India's container traffic.
points: Deendayal (Kandla) port, at the head of the Gulf of Kachchh, was developed as a major port to ease pressure on Mumbai after the loss of Karachi; it is a specially designed tidal port. It serves a highly productive granary and industrial belt across J&K, Himachal Pradesh, Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and Gujarat; it handles petroleum, fertilisers and other bulk cargo, with an offshore terminal at Vadinar for petroleum.

Mumbai port has a spacious natural harbour and is described by NCERT as the biggest port of the country (today Deendayal-Kandla and Paradip handle more cargo); it lies close to the general routes from the Middle East, Mediterranean countries, North Africa, North America and Europe; it has the country's largest oil terminal.
Mumbai's main hinterland includes Maharashtra, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan.
Jawaharlal Nehru Port (JNPT) at Nhava Sheva was developed as a satellite port to relieve pressure on Mumbai port; it is the largest container port in India.

topics.title: West coast ports II: Marmagao, New Mangalore and Kochi

learn.hook: Kochi, the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea', sits beside one of the world's busiest shipping lanes between Suez and Colombo.
points: Marmagao port, at the entrance of the Zuari estuary, is a natural harbour in Goa; it gained significance after remodelling in 1961 to handle iron ore exports to Japan; the Konkan Railway has considerably extended its hinterland (Karnataka, Goa, southern Maharashtra).

New Mangalore port, in Karnataka, caters to the export of iron ore and iron concentrates (from Kudremukh); it also handles fertilisers, petroleum products, edible oils, coffee, tea, wood pulp, yarn, granite and molasses; Karnataka is its major hinterland.
Kochi port, at the head of the Vembanad Kayal, is popularly known as the 'Queen of the Arabian Sea'; it is a natural harbour.
Kochi has an advantageous location close to the Suez–Colombo route; it caters to Kerala, southern Karnataka and south-western Tamil Nadu.

topics.title: East coast ports I: Kolkata, Haldia and Paradip

learn.hook: Kolkata port is not on the sea at all — it lies 128 km up the Hugli river, and ships fight silt to reach it.
points: Kolkata port is located on the Hugli river, 128 km inland from the Bay of Bengal; developed by the British, it had the early advantage of being at the capital of British India.

It faces silt accumulation in the Hugli and needs constant dredging; it has lost significance as exports were diverted to Visakhapatnam, Paradip and its satellite port Haldia. Its hinterland covers UP, Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Sikkim and the north-eastern states, and it serves landlocked Nepal and Bhutan.

Haldia port, 105 km downstream from Kolkata, was built to reduce congestion at Kolkata; it handles bulk cargo — iron ore, coal, petroleum and its products, fertilisers, jute and jute products, cotton and cotton yarn.

Paradip port, in the Mahanadi delta about 100 km from Cuttack, has the deepest harbour, especially suited for very large vessels; it mainly handles large-scale iron ore exports; its hinterland includes Odisha, Chhattisgarh and Jharkhand.

example.q: Why was Haldia port developed downstream of Kolkata?
steps: Kolkata is 128 km inland on the Hugli and suffers from silting and congestion.
Haldia, 105 km downstream, is nearer the sea and easier for larger ships to reach.
So it was built to reduce congestion at Kolkata and handle bulk cargo.
example.answer: To reduce congestion at Kolkata and handle bulk cargo nearer the sea

topics.title: East coast ports II: Visakhapatnam, Chennai, Ennore and Tuticorin

learn.hook: Visakhapatnam's inner harbour is landlocked — ships enter through a channel cut through solid rock!
points: Visakhapatnam port (Andhra Pradesh) is a landlocked harbour connected to the sea by a channel cut through solid rock and sand; an outer harbour handles iron ore, petroleum and general cargo; Andhra Pradesh is its main hinterland.

Chennai port is one of the oldest ports on the east coast; it is an artificial harbour built in 1859; it is not very suitable for large ships because of shallow waters near the coast; Tamil Nadu and Puducherry are its hinterland.
Ennore (now Kamarajar) port was developed 25 km north of Chennai to relieve pressure on Chennai port.

V.O. Chidambaranar (Tuticorin) port, in Tamil Nadu, was also developed to relieve pressure on Chennai; it has a natural harbour and rich hinterland and handles coal, salt, foodgrains, edible oils, sugar, chemicals and petroleum products; it serves trade with Sri Lanka, the Maldives and coastal India.

learn.hook: Smoke from a chimney, a pesticide in a stream, a blaring horn and plastic in a field — four different kinds of pollution.
points: Environmental pollution results from the release of substances and energy from waste products of human activities, which harm the natural environment.
Pollution is classified by the medium through which pollutants are transported and diffused: air pollution, water pollution, land pollution and noise pollution.
Pollutants can be classified by origin (natural or human) and by how they travel; they move through air, water and soil, often from one medium to another.
Human activities, not natural processes, are the main cause of concern.

learn.hook: A tannery in Kanpur, a pesticide spray in Punjab, and lakhs of pilgrims at a ghat — all can pollute the same river.
points: Indiscriminate use of water by a growing population and industrial expansion has seriously degraded water quality.

Pollutants come from natural sources (erosion, landslides, decay and decomposition of plants and animals) but those from human activities are the real cause of concern; human sources are industrial, agricultural and cultural.

Industrial pollutants: industrial wastes, polluted waste water, poisonous gases, chemical residues, heavy metals, dust and smoke; most industrial waste is dumped into running water or lakes. Leather, pulp and paper, textiles and chemicals are major polluting industries.
Agricultural sources: inorganic fertilisers, pesticides and herbicides are washed into rivers, lakes and tanks, and seep into groundwater.
Cultural activities like pilgrimages, religious fairs and tourism also pollute water (e.g. bathing, immersion of idols, offerings, waste left by crowds).

example.answer: Industrial, agricultural, cultural, natural

topics.title: Effects of water pollution, the Ganga and Namami Gange

learn.hook: About one in four communicable diseases in India spreads through water. Clean rivers mean healthy people.
points: Polluted water causes water-borne diseases such as diarrhoea, intestinal worms and hepatitis; about one-fourth of communicable diseases in India are water-borne.

The Ganga has highly polluted stretches near cities like Kanpur, Allahabad (Prayagraj), Varanasi, Patna and Kolkata (industrial and urban effluents); the Yamuna is badly polluted around Delhi, Mathura and Agra.

The Namami Gange Programme (2014), under the National Mission for Clean Ganga, includes: sewerage treatment systems in towns, monitoring of industrial effluents, river-front development, afforestation along the banks, cleaning of the river surface, developing 'Ganga Grams' in Uttarakhand, UP, Bihar, Jharkhand and West Bengal, and public awareness to avoid adding pollutants even through rituals.
Activity: survey a local river or pond and list its pollution sources — sewage outfalls, factory drains, farm runoff, solid waste, washing and bathing.

example.q: A student surveys a local pond and sees a drain from houses, plastic waste, washing of clothes and cattle bathing. List the pollution sources and one solution for each.
steps: Household drain → sewage: divert to treatment.
Plastic waste → solid waste: collection and ban on dumping.
Washing clothes (detergents) → separate washing area.
Cattle bathing → separate cattle trough.
example.answer: Sewage, solid waste, detergents, animal waste — with treatment, collection and separation

learn.hook: Every winter, Delhi's air turns grey and schools sometimes shut. What is in that smog?
points: Air pollution is the addition of contaminants like dust, fumes, gas, fog, odour, smoke or vapour to the air in substantial proportion and duration that may be harmful to flora, fauna and property.
Main sources: combustion of fossil fuels, mining and industries; they release oxides of sulphur and nitrogen, hydrocarbons, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, lead and asbestos.
Effects: air pollution causes diseases of the respiratory, nervous and circulatory systems.
Smoky fog over cities, called urban smog, is caused by atmospheric pollution and is very harmful to health; air pollution can also cause acid rain.

learn.hook: A pressure horn can blast over 100 decibels — loud enough to damage hearing over time.
points: Noise pollution is the state of unbearable and uncomfortable noise caused by various sources.
Sources: factories, mechanised construction and demolition works, automobiles and aircraft, sirens, loudspeakers and noise during festivals.

Noise is measured in decibels (dB). The biggest nuisance is traffic noise, whose intensity depends on the type of vehicle, aircraft or train and the condition of roads and vehicles; in sea traffic, noise is confined to harbours.

Effects: hearing impairment, stress, irritation and sleep disturbance. Noise pollution is location-specific: its intensity declines with distance from the source, and it is hazardous in metropolitan and big cities, industrial areas and along transport routes.

topics.title: Urban waste disposal: sources and problems

learn.hook: Mountains of garbage like Delhi's Ghazipur landfill rise as tall as some buildings. Where does all that waste come from?
points: Urban areas are marked by overcrowding, congestion and inadequate facilities to support fast-growing populations, leading to poor sanitation and foul air — serious environmental and health problems.

Solid wastes are old and used articles (rusted metal, broken glass, plastic containers, polythene bags, ashes, paper, food waste etc.) from two main sources: household or domestic establishments, and industrial or commercial establishments.
Household waste is often dumped on public land or private contractors' sites; industrial solid waste is disposed of in low-lying public grounds (landfills).

Problems: foul smell, and flies and rodents that carry diseases like typhoid, diphtheria, diarrhoea, malaria and cholera; carelessly handled waste is spread by wind and washed by rainwater, causing nuisance.

topics.title: Urban waste disposal: pollution and solutions

learn.hook: If every home in India separated wet and dry waste, compost and recycling could handle most city garbage. It starts at your kitchen bin!
points: Industrial solid waste and untreated urban sewage are dumped into rivers, contaminating them; many towns lack sewage treatment facilities.
A large share of urban waste remains uncollected or is not processed, so collection and management systems need to be improved.
Waste can be treated as a resource: biodegradable waste can be composted or used to generate energy (biogas, waste-to-energy plants); recyclable waste can be recovered.
Segregation at source (wet and dry waste), recycling, reducing plastic use and community participation are key solutions.
The Swachh Bharat Mission (launched in 2014) promotes cleanliness, solid waste management and toilets in cities and villages.

learn.hook: Ramesh left his village to work as a welder in a big city, sending money home every month. His story is the story of millions.
points: Rural-urban migration results from high demand for labour in urban areas, low job opportunities and low wages in rural areas, and the unbalanced pattern of development between villages and cities.
Most migrants are unskilled or semi-skilled; many settle in slums and squatter settlements, putting pressure on urban infrastructure — housing, water, sanitation and transport.
Migration is often male-selective: men migrate alone, leaving women, children and the elderly in villages, which increases the burden of work and responsibility on women.

NCERT's narrative of Ramesh, a rural migrant working as a welder in a city, shows push factors (poverty, lack of work), pull factors (jobs, better wages), informal employment with little security, and remittances sent home to support his family.

steps: Push: drought, lack of jobs in the village.

Effect: remittances support his family; city slums and services face more pressure.

learn.hook: Dharavi in Mumbai is one of Asia's largest slums — yet inside its narrow lanes, potters, leather workers and recyclers run a busy economy.
points: Indian cities show a dualistic picture: well-developed planned colonies on one side and slums, jhuggi-jhopri clusters and shanty towns on the other.

Slums are the least preferred residential areas: dilapidated houses, poor hygiene and ventilation, and lack of basic amenities like drinking water, light and toilets; they are overcrowded with narrow lanes and are prone to serious fire hazards.

Most slum dwellers work in low-paid, high-risk jobs in the unorganised sector; many are undernourished, prone to illness and unable to afford proper education for their children; poverty makes them vulnerable to drug abuse, alcoholism, crime and social exclusion.

Case study — Dharavi (Mumbai): one of Asia's largest slums, with narrow lanes, congested houses, poor drainage and sanitation; yet it has a large informal economy — pottery, leather goods, garments, recycling — and a hard-working, resilient community.
Solutions include slum upgradation and rehabilitation: in-situ redevelopment, affordable housing (e.g. PMAY-Urban), and providing water, sanitation, electricity and secure tenure.

example.q: List three problems faced by slum dwellers and one solution for each.
steps: Lack of toilets and clean water → provide community toilets and piped water.
Fire hazards in congested lanes → wider lanes, safer materials, fire services.
Low-paid insecure jobs → skill training and access to social security.
example.answer: Poor amenities, fire risk, insecure work — with services, safer planning and skills

learn.reallife: Dharavi's recycling units process large amounts of Mumbai's plastic and metal waste — showing the economic energy of slum communities.

learn.hook: In Madhya Pradesh's Jhabua district, Bhil communities turned bare, eroded hills green again through watershed work.
points: Land degradation is the temporary or permanent decline in the productive capacity of land due to natural and human causes.
Limited availability of agricultural land increases pressure on it; degraded land is often called wasteland.
Naturally created wastelands: gullied or ravinous land, desertic or coastal sands, barren rocky areas, steep sloping land and glacial areas.
Human-induced wastelands: waterlogged and marshy areas, land affected by salinity and alkalinity, degraded forests, degraded pastures and grazing land, and mining and industrial wastelands.

Measures: afforestation, check dams and contour bunding, soil conservation, controlled grazing and watershed management with people's participation (e.g. Jhabua, MP). Exam focus: pollution types and sources, Namami Gange, urban waste, slums, migration and land degradation.
